While Vortigern <note>A legendary 5th-century king of the Britons, often blamed for inviting the Saxons into Britain.</note>, King of the Britons, was sitting upon the bank of a drained pool, two dragons emerged, one of which was white, and the other truly red. And when one had approached the other, they engaged in a terrible battle, and they breathed out fire with their breath. However, the white dragon was prevailing, and chased the red one all the way to the edge of the lake. But the red dragon, when he grieved that he had been driven out, made an attack upon the white one, and forced him to retreat. Therefore, as they were fighting in this manner, the King commanded Ambrose Merlin <note>The famous wizard of Arthurian legend; in this version, Geoffrey of Monmouth combines the stories of a prophetic child named Ambrose with the legends of Merlin.</note> to say what the battle of the dragons <term>portended</term> <note>original: "portendebat" — meaning to signify or foreshadow a future event.</note>. Soon he, bursting into tears, drew in the spirit of Prophecy, and said: “Woe to the red dragon: For his destruction hastens. The white dragon, who represents the Saxons <note>The Germanic tribes who migrated to and eventually conquered much of Britain.</note> whom you invited, shall occupy his caverns. The red dragon, however, designates the people of Britain, who shall be oppressed by the white one; its mountains, therefore, as [the valleys...]

# THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

...the goat of the Castle of Venus <note>original: "Venerij castri" — this likely refers to a location associated with luxury or perhaps a specific castle such as Scarborough, but here it serves to introduce a period of decadence</note>, having golden horns and a silver beard, who shall breathe out such a great cloud from his nostrils that the entire surface of the island shall be overshadowed. Women shall become like serpents in their gait, and every step they take shall be filled with pride. The castles of Venus shall be renewed, nor shall the arrows of Cupid cease to wound. 

A fountain shall be turned into blood, and two kings shall engage in a duel because of a lioness at the Ford of the Staff <note>original: "vado baculi" — a Latin wordplay on the city of Stafford (Staff-ford)</note>. All the ground shall grow lush, and humanity shall not cease its lewdness. Three ages shall witness all these things, until the buried kings in the city of London shall be brought to light. Famine shall return again, mortality shall return, and the citizens shall grieve the desolation of their cities. 

Then shall come the Boar of Commerce <note>original: "aper commertij" — often interpreted by medieval commentators as a symbol of London's mercantile power or a king who restores the currency</note>, who shall call back the scattered flocks to their lost pastures. His breast shall be food for the needy, and his tongue shall quiet the thirsty. From his mouth shall flow rivers which shall water the parched throats of men. 

Thereafter, a tree shall be brought forth upon the Tower of London; content with only three branches, it shall nevertheless overshadow the surface of the entire island with the breadth of its leaves. Against it, the adversary Boreas <note>the North Wind, often symbolizing an invasion or threat from the North</note> shall come, and with his wicked blast he shall snatch away the third branch. But the two remaining branches shall occupy the place of the one torn away, until one branch shall annihilate the other by the sheer multitude of its leaves. Then that branch shall obtain the place of both and shall support the birds of foreign regions. To the birds of the native fatherland it shall be considered harmful, for through fear of its shadow they shall lose their freedom of flight. 

There shall succeed an Ass of Wickedness, swift against the makers [of gold]... <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "auri" (of gold) suggests the next page discusses counterfeiters or the debasement of currency.</note>

But when such great calamity has ceased, a detestable bird shall approach the valley of <term>Galabes|A mythical location, often identified as a fountain or sacred site in the woods of Wales where Merlin was said to have been found</term>, and shall lift it up into a high mountain. The fox shall devour its mother and shall bear an ass's head. Having thus taken on this monstrous form, it shall terrify its brothers and shall drive them into <term>Neustria|The western part of the Frankish kingdom, roughly corresponding to modern-day Normandy in France</term>. Soon the boar itself shall approach the corpse, and while standing over it, shall breathe into its eyes and face. 

But the fox, not forgetting her past trickery, shall bite his left foot and tear it entirely from his body. Making a leap, she shall also snatch away his right ear and tail, and hide within the caverns of the mountains. Therefore, the deceived boar shall seek the wolf and the bear, so that they might restore his lost limbs. When they have taken up the cause, they shall promise him two feet, ears, and a tail, and from these, they shall assemble <term>swinish limbs|original: "porcina membra"</term>. 

But the boar shall rest and wait for the promised restoration. Meanwhile, the fox shall descend from the mountains and transform itself into a wolf, and as if intending to hold a conversation with the boar, shall approach him cunningly and devour him entirely. After that, it shall transform itself into a boar, and as if without limbs, it shall wait for its brothers; but even these, after they have arrived, it shall kill with a sudden tooth, and it shall be crowned with the head of a lion.

The dragon of <term>Worcester|Latin: Wigornia</term> shall rise against him and attempt to destroy him; however, once they have clashed, the dragon shall be overcome and oppressed by the wickedness of the victor. For the giant shall mount the dragon and, casting off his clothes, sit upon it naked. The dragon shall carry him to the heights and, with tail erect, shall lash the naked rider. Regaining his strength, the giant shall shatter the dragon's jaws with a sword. At last, the dragon shall become entangled beneath its own tail and perish from its own venom. 

After him, the boar of <term>Totnes|Latin: Totonesius; a town in Devon</term> shall succeed and oppress the people with a dire tyranny. <term>Gloucester|Latin: Claudiocestria</term> shall bring forth a lion who will harass the serpent in various battles. He shall trample the serpent under his feet and terrify it with his gaping jaws. At length, the lion shall quarrel with the kingdom and shall climb over the backs of the nobles. A bull shall arrive at the dispute and strike the lion with its right hoof. It shall drive the lion through the various quarters of the kingdom, but the bull shall shatter its horns against the walls of <term>Exeter|Latin: Exonia</term>. 

The fox of <term>Kaerdubal|Likely Cardiff or Cardigan</term> shall avenge the lion and consume the bull entirely with its teeth. The adder of <term>Lincoln|Latin: Lindecolinus</term> shall coil around the fox, and shall announce its presence to many dragons with a terrifying hiss. The dragons shall clash, and one shall tear the other to pieces. The winged dragon shall overwhelm the wingless one, sinking its venomous claws into its cheeks.

<meta>This page continues the preface by Alan of Lille. In the preceding text, Alan established his qualifications as a scholar of British and European history. ### PREFACE.

...things. Therefore, from the beginning of the book until the end of the **British sovereignty**, and the beginning of the **kingdom of the English**, and thereafter until the return of the **British diaspora** <note>original: "Britannicæ dispersionis"; this refers to the medieval legend that the displaced Britons (the Welsh and Bretons) would one day reclaim the island of Britain from the Anglo-Saxons and Normans</note> into the Island of their fathers, I have explained the **oracles of Merlin** according to the truth of histories and the events of things, as best and as most plausibly as I could.

Furthermore, concerning those things which he predicts will happen after these in the same kingdom—as elsewhere—because they do not yet seem fulfilled, but are rather expected to be fulfilled in times yet to come: since histories do not prophesy the future, but rather narrate what has already been done, I have devoted myself to investigating the understanding of his sayings. I have done this not according to the lines of history and recorded deeds, but rather according to the **figures and tropes of prophetic speech**, the meanings of the words, and also according to the **natures and properties of the things themselves** from which the **Prophet Merlin** draws his metaphors. 

He often uses these names to call upon those whom he does not name by their proper names. What is more, I have followed the idiom and manner of speaking which I have noted—with careful consideration—that he maintains throughout the whole context of his work. In this, I believe I have inflicted no violence upon the literal text, inventing nothing discordant or absurd throughout the entire interpretation. Finally, I have devised nothing that seems foreign to the proper meanings of the words, or to the figurative and customary <term>translations|Latin: translationibus; in a rhetorical sense, this refers to metaphors or the "carrying over" of meaning from one word to another</term> of the terms. 

Otherwise, those who come after us will understand and know more certainly and clearly those things which will happen in their own respective times,

### PRÆFATIO.

...come to his prophecies, we prove that they have run their course and been fulfilled up to the present day, according to what the sequence of histories and the events of the things themselves declare. Indeed, it is most certain that he was a Christian, since he was of the British nation; and more than two hundred years before he was born, all Britain was converted from the **error of many gods** <note>original: "multideo errore"; referring to pagan polytheism</note> to the worship of the one true God through its King Lucius, by the legates of Pope Eleutherius and their preaching, and was renewed by holy baptism. By what spirit he prophesied, however, only that highest God of spirits knows, who has always caused or permitted those things He willed to be prophesied and foretold in every nation and people, through whom He willed, before they came to pass.

<margin>Job chapter 19 verse 25</margin>
Finally, **Job** was neither a Christian nor a Jew, but certainly a **Gentile** <note>original: "gentilis"; here meaning a non-Israelite or pagan who nonetheless worshipped the true God</note>, and yet I find that none of the prophets prophesied more clearly or faithfully concerning Christ and the resurrection of us all on the last day. *I know, he said, that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God my Savior. ### PREFACE.

...and we have known her to have prophesied about his second coming to judgment, the **end of the age** <note>original: "consummatione seculi"</note>, the resurrection of all, the glory of the Saints, and the damnation of the wicked. Thus the holy **Doctors of the Church** <note>the influential early Christian theologians</note>, and especially **Augustine**, were not ashamed to include her prophecies in their books and to proclaim them in the Church as testimony for Christ. **Virgil** also mentions this prophecy in that *Eclogue* in which Augustine testifies that he, too, prophesied about the **incarnation of Christ** <note>the belief that God became human in Jesus</note>. Indeed, the beginning of that *Eclogue* sufficiently suggests that he is about to sing of a great mystery. For it begins thus:

Finally, Apuleius <note>a 2nd-century North African philosopher and author</note>, in the book titled *On the God of Socrates*, asserts that between the Moon and the earth dwell demons, whom they call **Incubi**. So too Plato says that there is a certain kind of demon between the Moon and the earth in this moist part of the air, which is defined as: A moist animal, rational, immortal, and subject to emotion <note>original: *passibile*, meaning capable of feeling passion or suffering</note>. It is the nature of this being to envy man; because from where the demon fell through pride, man ascends through humility. 

Some of these beings are so lustful that sometimes, taking on a human likeness, they mingle with women and procreate. For this reason, they are called **Incubi**. The Romans call them *Fauni sicarii* <note>original: *sicarios*, literally "assassins," though in this context it may be a corruption of *ficarii*, referring to fig-tree spirits associated with lust</note>. WHILE Vortigern <note>A 5th-century warlord and King of the Britons</note>, King of the Britons, was sitting upon the bank of a drained pool, two dragons emerged, one of which was white, and the other indeed red. And when one had approached the other, they engaged in a dreadful battle, and they breathed forth fire with their breath. However, the white dragon was prevailing, and was driving the red one to the edge of the lake. But the red dragon, when it grieved that it had been driven out, made an attack upon the white one, and forced it to go back. Therefore, while they were fighting in this manner, the king commanded Merlin Ambrosius <note>The name "Ambrosius" links the prophet to the historical figure Aurelius Ambrosius; in legend, Merlin is often called Merlin Ambrosius</note> to say what the battle of the dragons portended. Presently, he burst into weeping: he drew in the Spirit of prophecy, and having taken up a parable, he said: *“Woe to the Red Dragon: for its destruction hastens. The White Dragon shall occupy its caves, which signifies the Saxons <note>Germanic tribes whose arrival in Britain is a central theme of this era</note>, whom you invited. But the Red Dragon designates the race of the Britons, which shall be oppressed by the white one. Its mountains and valleys shall be made level, and the rivers of the valleys shall flow with blood. The practice of religion shall be destroyed, and the ruin of the Churches shall be clear to see. At last, the oppressed race shall prevail, and shall resist the cruelty of the foreigners, etc.”*

### BOOK I.

Vortigern, King of the Britons, after he had been deceived by the Saxons whom he had invited from Germany to his aid, and had lost almost all of Britain, on the advice of his diviners ordered a very strong tower to be built on a certain mountain, in the borders of Loegria <note>The medieval Latin name for England, derived from the Welsh *Lloegr*</note> and Wales, which would serve as a defense for him. But when the stone foundations were laid, they suddenly vanished, swallowed up by the earth. The King, astonished, sought the cause from his magicians. Then they, blushing to confess their ignorance, claimed that the structure could not stand unless the stones and mortar were sprinkled with the blood of a murdered man who had been born without a human father.

Therefore, servants were sent through various regions to seek out such a man. When some of them had come to a certain city in Wales called Kaër Merdin <note>Modern-day Carmarthen; the text explains the name as "the city of Merlin"</note>—that is, the city of Merlin, with the letter 'l' changed into 'd' <note>original: "l. litera versa in d."</note>—they saw boys playing together before the city gate. A quarrel arose between two of them, one of whom was named Merlin, and the other Dinabutius. 

Among other insults, Dinabutius reproached Merlin for not having a father. Hearing this, the envoys questioned the bystanders as to who the boy was. They replied that it was not known who had fathered him; however, his mother was the daughter of the King of Demetia <note>A kingdom in South Wales, roughly modern-day Pembrokeshire and Carmarthenshire</note> and was a nun in the Church of Saint Peter in that city. Having heard these things, the envoys approached the governor of the city, and by his order, they brought Merlin and his mother to the King. When she was questioned separately by the King as to which man she had conceived Merlin by, she said; that [the] man...

# THE PROPHECY OF MERLIN

...[that she] had known no other man, except that while she was in her chambers among her companions, a very strong young man in human form appeared to her several times when he found her alone. After kissing her many times, he would suddenly vanish. Finally, however, she was overpowered by him and conceived Merlin. 

When Merlin had heard all this, he said to the king: "The magicians who gave you such advice are utterly ignorant of what lies hidden beneath the mountain, which causes the stone foundations to be swallowed up." He ordered that the workmen be called to dig into the earth, where they would find a pool <note>original: "stagnum"</note> that was washing away the stones; at the bottom of the pool, they would find two hollow stones, and within them, two sleeping dragons. 

By the king's command, the earth was dug, the pool was found and drained, and the hollow stones were found and opened. Two dragons emerged—one red and the other white—and began a terrible fight. The king, amazed, asked Merlin what their battle foretold. Then Merlin, bursting into tears and filled with the spirit of prophecy, said: 

*“Woe to the red dragon, for its destruction hastens. The white dragon shall occupy its caverns; it represents the Saxons whom you invited.”* 

By "the caverns of the red dragon," he refers to the cities, towns, and houses of the Britons, keeping with the metaphor of dragons who live in caves. The red dragon designates the people of Britain, who will be oppressed by the white dragon—that is, the Saxons. 

*“Its mountains and valleys shall be made level,”* meaning that a shared misfortune will bring the high and the low to the same state. 

*“And the rivers of the valleys shall flow with blood”*; this is spoken hyperbolically <note>This refers to a figure of speech involving exaggeration for emphasis, suggesting the scale of the coming slaughter.</note>

This was indeed carried out; thus, Constans was called King in name only, while Vortigern managed all affairs, both domestic and foreign, according to his own will. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the legendary encounter between Saint Patrick and the unborn Saint David, explaining why Merlin’s prophecy presents these events in a chronologically reversed order through the rhetorical device of anticipation.</meta>

# BOOK I.
## C 3

...for when he had visited the brothers there according to custom, he was seized by a sudden weakness and passed to the Lord, and was buried there. Regarding the statement: *Menevia <note>St Davids, the cathedral city in Pembrokeshire, Wales.</note> shall be clothed in the <term>pallium</term> <note>A woolen vestment given by the Pope to archbishops, symbolizing their authority.</note> of the City of Legions <note>Caerleon, the ancient Roman fortress in South Wales and the former seat of the Welsh archdiocese.</note>*, and the later addition, *and the preacher of Ireland <note>Saint Patrick, whom the text claims was silenced by the spiritual presence of the unborn Saint David.</note> shall become silent because of the infant growing in the womb*, the order is reversed. This is because, in the prophetic manner, the author chose to represent later events through <term>anticipation</term> <note>Known in rhetoric as prolepsis; the representation of a future act as if it were already completed, or switching the natural order of events.</note>, and placed earlier events afterward.

This figure of speech is very common in both secular and divine scriptures; specifically, when things that occur later are spoken of first, or future things are presented as if they were already past. We see this in Virgil: *Meanwhile the kings with a massive escort, Latinus proceed.* <note>original: "Interea reges ingenti mole, Latinus procedunt." From the Aeneid, Book 12. The grammar suggests the escort and the king move together, though the "kings" are mentioned before the singular "Latinus" is specified.</note> Indeed, the sense and order of the words is: "Meanwhile King Latinus proceeds with a massive escort—that is, with great dignity—and after him the other kings."

Likewise: *Then they prepare to parch with flames and break with stone,* <note>original: "Tunc torrere parant flammis & frangere Saxo." From the Aeneid, Book 1. This describes preparing grain for food.</note> even though the grain is first broken by the stone—that is, the millstone—and afterward cooked by the fire. A similar example is found in the Psalm: *His foundations are in the holy mountains, the Lord loves the gates of Sion above all the tabernacles of Jacob.* <note>original: "Fundamenta eius in montibus sanctis, diligit Dominus portas Sion, super omnia tabernacula Iacob." Psalm 87.</note> He placed the word "His" first, and only afterward identified to whom it refers—that is, Sion—when it should have been said: "The foundations of Sion are in these mountains; the Lord loves its gates above all the tabernacles of Jacob."

Likewise: *they divided my garments among them, and for my vesture they cast lots* <note>original: "diuiserunt sibi vestimenta mea, & super vestem meam miserunt sortem." Psalm 22.</note> instead of "they divide" and "they cast." So also in Genesis, when Moses said through anticipation, *let us make man in our image and likeness* <note>original: "faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram." Genesis 1:26.</note>, adding from the person of the Father, *so that he may rule over the fish...*

# PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

*...of the sea, and the birds of the sky, and the beasts of the earth, and every creature, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth. And God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. And God blessed them and said: "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the sky, and all living things that move upon the earth." And God said: "Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed upon the earth, and all trees which have in themselves the ordering of their own kind, that they may be food for you, and for all the animals of the earth, and every bird of the sky, and all things that move upon the earth and in which there is a living soul, so that they may have them to eat." Yet later, after a few other things are interjected, it says: "These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created, in the day that the Lord God made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it rose up in the earth, and every herb of the region before it germinated. For the Lord God had not yet rained upon the earth, and there was no man to work the soil," and so forth.* <note>The author is quoting the Latin Vulgate version of Genesis 1:26–30 and 2:4–5. He uses this as a "proof of concept": Genesis 1 describes plants and humans as already created, while Genesis 2 later describes the earth before plants had germinated or man existed. This justifies Merlin’s non-linear prophetic style.</note>

The writings of the poets and our own sacred scriptures are full of figures of speech of this kind, which any diligent reader will easily find in many places. In this same way, the "correct" order of the words in Merlin’s prophecy would have followed the natural sequence of events if he had spoken thus: *The preacher of Ireland <note>Saint Patrick.</note> shall become silent because of the infant growing in the womb <note>Saint David.</note>. The seventh Pastor of York <note>Referring to an archbishop of York; the "seventh" likely refers to a specific historical or legendary succession.</note> shall be frequented in the kingdom of Armorica <note>The ancient name for Brittany, France, where many British clergy fled during the Anglo-Saxon invasions.</note>, London shall adorn Canterbury <note>original: "Doroberniam." In the Middle Ages, Canterbury was often called Dorobernia.</note>, and Menevia <note>St Davids in Wales.</note> shall be clothed in the <term>pallium</term> <note>A vestment signifying archepiscopal authority.</note> of the City of Legions <note>Caerleon; the prophecy suggests the transfer of the archbishop's seat from the Roman city of Caerleon to St Davids.</note>.*

But I do not recall finding in the annals that anything like this happened before or since, especially on that island. Therefore, by "bloody rain" he means the shedding of human blood, caused sometimes by hostile wars and sometimes by civil discords, as if a rain of blood were falling from the sky—that is, dripping down from heavenly vengeance. This was followed by a dire famine afflicting mortals, as is read in the deeds of the Britons, so that nothing at all could be found to be taken as food, except only the comfort of the hunter's craft.

### THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

*You shall sow much seed in the earth and gather little, because locusts will devour everything. You shall plant and dig a vineyard, but you shall not drink the wine, nor collect anything from it, because it will be laid waste by worms. You shall have olives in all your borders, yet you shall not be anointed with oil, because they will drop off and perish. Mildew shall consume all your trees and the fruits of your land. The stranger who lives among you shall rise above you and be higher, while you shall descend and be lower. He shall be the head, and you shall be the tail. And all these curses shall come upon you, and those pursuing shall overtake you, until you perish. You shall serve your enemy, whom the Lord will send against you, in hunger and thirst and nakedness, and in every want; and he shall place an iron yoke upon your neck, until he crushes you.* <note>The author is quoting the "Curses of Disobedience" from the Book of Deuteronomy (28:38–48) to provide a biblical parallel to the hardships faced by the Britons.</note>

<margin>Cadwallo, King of the Britons.</margin>
The history of the Britons clearly declares that things similar to these in every respect happened to them during the time written above. And this is why the prophet says: *a bloody rain shall fall, and a dire famine shall afflict mortals.* And since he spoke of "mortals" indefinitely—meaning those to be afflicted by the starvation of famine—he specifies in the following discourse which mortals he means: that is, the race of the Britons. This is what he adds: *at the arrival of these things, the Red [Dragon] shall grieve*—understand the "Dragon," <note>original: "draco"</note> that is, the race of the Britons—*but it shall thrive through immense labor.* This signifies that the Britons were first to be worn down by the cruelty of wars and the starvation of famine, but afterward, they would prevail through the immense labors of those same wars. This restoration of happiness <note>original: "beatitudo"</note> came to them through Cadwallo <note>Cadwallon ap Cadfan (d. 634), a King of Gwynedd who led a major, though ultimately temporary, British resurgence against the Anglo-Saxons.</note> their King, by a turn of fortune's wheel, following inexplicable evils, expulsions from their ancestral soil, and dispersions through foreign places.

The inextricable labyrinths of his labors—

### BOOK I.

<margin>Year of Christ 633.</margin>
To unfold these events in detail is a matter of history. For here Cadwallo, after many misfortunes and horrors, after various exiles, and finally after his expulsion from his own kingdom and the loss of the entire island, sailed to Lesser Britain <note>Lesser Britain refers to Brittany in modern-day France, which served as a refuge for Britons fleeing the Anglo-Saxon advance.</note> with the few who remained with him. He went to implore the aid of King Solomon, his kinsman, and his fellow brothers. Assisted by them, he hoped to be able to turn back his sails, return to his homeland, and recover the kingdom of Northumbria <note>original: *Northanhumbriæ*</note> which had been snatched from him by King Edwin. Having obtained this help, and after spending the winter with Solomon, he set out when spring returned—the time when kings are accustomed to go forth to war. Cadwallo boarded his ships with ten thousand soldiers whom King Solomon had entrusted to him, and using a favorable wind, he arrived after a swift voyage.

When he heard that Penda, King of the Mercians, was encircling his nephew Brian and the miserable remnants of the Britons in a siege at Exeter <note>original: *Exonia*</note>, he hurried there tirelessly. Having divided his soldiers into troops, he did not delay in attacking the enemy. In the thick of the battle, Penda was captured. Since he had no other way to ensure his safety, Penda submitted himself to Cadwallo, giving hostages to maintain his loyalty. He even gave Cadwallo his daughter in marriage, and thus became the King's father-in-law and the commander of his army <note>original: *princeps militiæ*</note>.

From there, Cadwallo recalled the Britons to the island, who for a long time had been dispersed through various places. He led his army into Northumbria against King Edwin, and devastated the homeland with the sword <note>original: *ferro*, literally "iron"</note> and plunder. Nor did Edwin remain sluggishly idle...

...dence of those things which follow, let us return to the sequence of the letter <note>That is, the literal text of the prophecy.</note>, briefly running over those things whose explanation we have already provided beforehand. *A bloody rain shall fall, and a dire famine shall consume mortals.* Because of these impending things, the Red <note>The Red Dragon represents the Britons.</note> shall grieve, but shall thrive with immense labor. It follows: *Seven scepter-bearers shall be slain, and one of them shall be sanctified.* The seven scepter-bearers whom Cadwallo and Penda, his father-in-law, slew, were Edwin, Osric <note>original: *Offricus*; referring to the King of Deira.</note>, and Oswald, Kings of Northumbria; and Sigeberht, Ecgric, and Anna, who reigned over the East Angles, their kingdom's borders being divided.

Cadam, also the King of Scotland, overcome by equal hardship, perished. Out of all these, he says that one specifically shall be sanctified: meaning the Blessed Oswald, a man of great faith in God and of great gentleness toward his people, 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus chapter 45, verse 4. Hebrews chapter 11, verse 6.</margin> 
according to that scripture: *in his faith and gentleness, He made him holy.* <note>original: *in fide & lenitate ipſius, ſanctum fecit illum.*</note> For just as without faith it is impossible to please God, as the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> says, so too is it impossible to please men without gentleness. In whomever these two things harmonize and align equally—that is, right faith toward God and meekness of spirit toward one's neighbor—that person is without doubt a saint, beloved by God and men: whose memory is in blessing, having been made like to the glory of the saints.

# THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

<margin>Psalm 111 verse 9. 2 Corinthians 9.</margin>
The histories of the English report that the Blessed Oswald, King of Northumbria, was such a man, and they pursue his praises in a panegyric <note>A panegyric is a formal speech or piece of writing designed to highly praise someone.</note> style of writing. For you will easily notice how much fervor of faith burned in his breast from this fact: if ever Bishop Aidan <note>original: *Aldanus*; referring to Saint Aidan of Lindisfarne.</note>—who, being a Scot, spoke in the Scottish tongue <note>The "Scottish tongue" here refers to Old Irish or Gaelic.</note>—preached the word of God in the Church of God to those standing by, and an interpreter was missing, the King himself would immediately take up that duty. Though he was dressed in a cloak either stiff with gold or saturated with linen dyes and glowing with Tyrian purple <note>original: *tyrios murices*; a costly purple dye derived from sea snails, a symbol of high royalty.</note>, he worthily took up the task of explaining the "envelope" of that foreign speech in his native tongue. He was so temperate toward himself and so generous toward the poor that often, when the side dishes were served and the guests sharpened their teeth and set their minds upon the food, he would restrain his own pleasure, filling the stomachs of the poor from his own scarcity and purchasing their joy by defrauding his own body of its needs. For this reason, I believe that even in this worldly life, the absolute truth of that heavenly oracle was fulfilled in him: *He has dispersed, he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains forever and ever.* <note>original: *disperfit, dedit pauperibus, iustitia eius manet in seculum seculi.* This is a quote from Psalm 112:9 (111 in the Vulgate) and 2 Corinthians 9:9.</note> For what the listener ought to marvel at, he cannot deny: that royal right hand, the servant of such great alms, remains today—along with the arm, the skin, and the nerves—uncorrupted, according to the prayer of Bishop Aidan. For when the Bishop was feasting with the King on the holy day of Easter, and the King, hearing the cry of the poor, sent them a silver dish full and packed with meat, commanding that they should indeed take the food...

Thereafter, the Red Dragon shall return to its own customs and labor to rage against itself. <note>In Merlin's prophecy, the Red Dragon represents the native Britons (the Welsh), while the White Dragon represents the Saxon invaders.</note> After the death of Cadwallon, the restless nation of the Britons, impatient for peace, returned to internal wars and civil discords. But they did not do so with impunity. For there follows a description of the evils that their unrestrained recklessness suffered. The vengeance of the Thunderer <note>original: *tonantis*; a classical poetic epithet for Jupiter, here used to signify the Christian God's divine wrath.</note> will arrive, and every field will deceive the farmers—that is, the harvest will fail them. A great mortality will seize the people and empty out all the nations. The survivors will desert their native soil. While the Britons were fighting amongst themselves in civil rebellion, a heavenly vengeance arrived, as a result of which foreigners <note>The Saxons.</note> returned to their cities and towns. Famine and plague also arrived, by which the remnants of the people were worn down. Those who survived such great evils fled to foreign nations, and this is what the prophecy means: *the remnants shall desert their native soil and sow crops in foreign lands.*

*The blessed king shall prepare a voyage, and in the twelfth hall, he shall be numbered among the blessed.* This refers to King Cadwaladr, the son of Cadwallon. During the aforementioned scattering of his people, he himself went to Alan, the king of Lesser Britain <note>Armorica, or modern-day Brittany in France.</note>, so that when such a deadly plague had ceased, he might, with Alan's help, restore the ancestral kingdom with his fellow Britons, who were scattered through various provinces

He was told instead to go to Sergius, the Roman Pope <term>Pontifex Romanus|The Pope in Rome; specifically Pope Sergius I (reigned 687–701 AD).</term>, so that, having received penance and being purified by him, he might deserve to enter the heavenly kingdom. He was informed, however, that by his own merits the Britons would rule again when the time predetermined by God should arrive—but only after his body had first been brought back by them from Rome to Britain. The Blessed King obeyed the heavenly oracle and, proceeding to Rome, was honorably received by Pope Sergius. Without delay, he was seized by a sudden illness and saw his final day in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 688 <note>original: "DCLXXXVIII". Historical records generally place Cadwaladr's death in 689 AD.</note>.

For indeed, it shall be in unrest and subjection for fifty <note>original: "L."</note> years, but it shall "sit" for three hundred. For nearly one hundred and fifty <note>original: "C. ferme & L."</note> years from the death of Cadwallon <note>Refers to Cadwallon ap Cadfan (died c. 634 AD) or his son Cadwaladr; the commentator here uses the timeline to mark the decline of British power.</note>, although the Britons were hiding in the forests of Wales and were subjected to the Saxons, they nevertheless made frequent and dire raids against them. As for the addition, *and it shall sit for three hundred years*, these three hundred years are not to be separated from the preceding one hundred and fifty years; rather, those one hundred and fifty years are included within the three hundred. Truly, there were three hundred years from the days of Cadwallon until the arrival of the Danes in England and the establishment of their kingdom over the English.

Therefore, for three hundred years the **Bronze Prince** <term>Bronze Prince|Latin: *aeneus princeps*. This means that, humbled and subjected under the yoke of the English, they shall sit in confusion and sadness. And so, for three hundred years, the Bronze Prince "sat"—that is, he was humbled and subjected under the power of the English. Having returned therefore for a third time, they brought ruin to the western province, which was until then untouched; monasteries were overturned, the city of Oxford <term>Oxonia|Oxford</term> was set on fire, Kent <term>Cantia|Kent</term> was given over to plundering, and the Metropolitan city of Canterbury <term>Cantuaria|Canterbury</term> was burned. But the Almighty glorified his martyr, such that even the barbarians who had advanced to kill him—after seeing a miracle in which a dry piece of wood smeared with his blood had turned green again in a single night—rushed eagerly to kiss the dead man and submissively bowed their necks, their barbarian ferocity subdued. To this very time, both his fresh blood and his whole body endure. 

And to be brief, they had already devastated nearly half of the kingdom with sword, flame, and plunder. Meanwhile, King Ethelred—a man "brave and vigorous," and beautifully suited for sleeping—weighed matters of business lightly and yawned. And if ever he tried to lift himself up even by an elbow, immediately, either burdened by laziness or opposed by fortune, he fell back miserably. The ghosts <note>original: "umbræ fraternę," referring to the spirit of his murdered brother, Edward the Martyr</note> of his brother hounded him, demanding dire funeral rites from his head. Finally, a plan was adopted to lighten the war with money: first twenty-four thousand pounds were weighed out, and not long after, thirty thousand. 

Thus, according to the prophecy of Merlin, the north wind [shall wither] the flowers <note>original: "aquilo flores," likely part of the prophecy "Exsurget aquilo et flores decutiet," meaning the North wind shall rise and shake off the flowers, symbolizing the Viking invasions from the North</note>

But there was not yet an end to these evils. For, encouraged by the incitements of the Danes, Sweyn <term>Suanus|Sweyn Forkbeard</term>, King of Denmark <term>Danomarchia|Denmark</term>, was inspired to seek England, intending to subject it to his power with little effort; for it was a noble and rich country. But he heard the king was snoring <note>A reference to King Ethelred "the Unready," whose nickname "Unræd" meant "bad counsel" but was often mocked as laziness</note>, being a man devoted to luxury and wine, thinking nothing at all of warlike matters, and therefore hateful to his own people and a laughingstock to foreigners. He heard the commanders were faithless, the provincial people were cowardly, and that they would yield at the first blare of the trumpets <note>original: "lituorum," though OCR reads "liuorum"</note>. Now, Sweyn was prone to bloodshed, and he did not need much encouragement before he immediately readied his ships and hastened his crossing. 

Having thus invaded England, he began to press the land with slaughter and plunder. But he did not rejoice for long; on the feast of the 
<margin>The Year of Christ 1014.</margin>
Purification of the Blessed Mary <note>February 2nd</note>, he breathed his last. It is said, moreover, that while he was depopulating the land of Saint Edmund <note>The area around Bury St Edmunds in Suffolk</note>, the same Martyr appeared to him in a vision. When the Saint mildly confronted him regarding the misery of his people, and Sweyn responded with insolent pride, the Martyr struck him on the head. Stricken by this pain, he passed away shortly thereafter. 

Hearing of this, Cnut <term>Cnuto|Cnut the Great</term> his son—having settled affairs in

...because after his death <note>Referring to the eventual end of the Saxon/Danish conflicts</note>, they were subjugated and conquered by the Neustrians—that is, the Normans—and having lost their liberty, they underwent perpetual servitude. And this is what the prophecy says: *It shall flourish at last for a little while: but the decimation of Neustria, that is, of Normandy, shall do harm.* 

Concerning this "decimation of Neustria" (meaning Normandy) which was harmful to the Germanic dragon <note>The "Germanic dragon" is the author’s term for the Anglo-Saxons</note>, various people suspect various things. Not knowing what they are talking about or what they are affirming, they devise falsehoods and lies from their own hearts, failing to return to the truth of history. 

This, therefore, is the truth: Æthelred <note>original: "Edelredus"; known as Æthelred the Unready</note>, King of the English, when he saw that he was no match for Sweyn <note>original: "Suano"; Sweyn Forkbeard</note>, King of the Danes, due to the desertion of his own people, and dared not stand his ground against him, sent his wife Emma into Normandy to Richard <note>Richard II, Duke of Normandy</note>, Duke of Normandy, whose sister she was. He sent her with their two children, Alfred and Edward <note>The future Edward the Confessor</note>, whom he had fathered by her; he himself followed them and was received with worthy veneration by Richard. 

He later sailed back to England, where not long after he died. His two sons, however, remained in Normandy with their mother. But when Cnut <note>original: "Cnuto"; Cnut the Great</note> had brought all England under his rule, desiring to win over the English to himself, he summoned Emma, the widow of King Æthelred, from Normandy and took her as his wife. He did this so that while the English paid the accustomed respect to their Lady, they might more easily endure the rule of the Danes. By her, he fathered a son, whom he called Harthacnut <note>original: "Hardacum"</note>. However, when Cnut died, his son Harold <note>Harold Harefoot</note>, born of his first wife, took up the rule.

Historical accounts say that the aforementioned Earl Godwin—a man of great power with many sons who were equally strong—was the standard-bearer of this treachery against Alfred and his companions. For later, on a certain day when he was at a banquet with King Edward and his son Harold, the conversation turned to Alfred, the King’s brother. Having said this, he was choked by the morsel he had put into his mouth and turned his eyes toward death. Then he was dragged from under the table by his son Harold, who was standing by the King, and was committed to burial. Thus, under God as judge, the blinding of Alfred and the decimation of his companions was meanwhile avenged upon the head of the man who had been the leader of that entire faction and wickedness. 

However, this was fulfilled more fully after the death of King Edward, when William, Duke of the Normans, came into England against Harold, the son of the aforementioned traitor Godwin. Upon the death of King Edward in London, Harold had violently seized the crown of the kingdom by extorting an oath of loyalty from the nobles on that very day, even though he was not of the royal line—except for the fact that King Edward had his sister as a wife. What this means is this: while the Danes still held the northern parts of England and York <note>original: "Eboracum"</note>—the metropolis of that region—along with the Scots and the English, and were laying waste to everything nearby, **William** <note>William the Conqueror</note>, having gathered a significant force of knights and infantry, hastened toward those regions without delay. He besieged and captured York, killed and expelled the barbarians, and restored the lost possessions to the former inhabitants—that is, the English—though the victory was not bloodless for him, as he had lost many of his own men in the fighting there. And this is what the prophecy means when it says: *He restores the possessions to the former inhabitants, and the ruin of the outsiders shall be manifest,* that is, the ruin of the Danes. 

Regarding them, it is further added: *The seed of the white dragon shall be scraped from our little gardens, and the remnants of its generation shall be decimated.* The "seed of the white dragon" <note>In Merlin’s prophecies, the white dragon usually symbolizes the Saxons or Germanic invaders, while the red dragon symbolizes the Britons.</note> refers to the Danes themselves, seeing as they came from Germany; they were "scraped" from the little gardens—that is, from the cities and towns that once belonged to the Britons—by **William**, as has been stated. ...since he was the firstborn, he <note>King William I</note> denied him <note>Robert Curthose</note> the kingdom. The reason for this was that Robert constantly allied himself with Philip, King of the **Franks**, who was troubling **Normandy**, and he pressed against his own homeland more sharply than the others. <margin>In the year 1087, on the 7th day of September.</margin>
Therefore, when William the father had died on the seventh ides of September <note>September 7th</note>, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1087—which was the 22nd year of his reign and the 59th of his life—his body was prepared with royal solemnity and carried along the **Seine** to **Caen** <note>original: "Cadomum"</note>, and buried there. And so, when his son **William** <note>William II, known as William Rufus</note> had begun to reign after the death of his father, his first conflict was against his paternal uncle **Odo**, the <term>Bishop of Bayeux</term> and also the <term>Earl of Kent</term>. Because Odo took it very poorly that his nephew Robert had been disinherited from the kingdom, he was the first to defect from the King, and he inclined many toward Robert—first with secret whispers, and later with manifest allegations. For he said that the kingdom belonged to the firstborn by right, and that Robert was likewise moved by merit, since he was a modest man who had already "boiled away" <note>original: "decoxiffet"—meaning he had matured or tempered his youthful recklessness through his many hardships.</note> his youthful follies through many labors. In contrast, he claimed William was puffed up and proud with a cruelty of spirit that he could not even hide in his face, and that he would dare everything against right and law with youthful impulse and the license of power. With these and similar persuasions, he withdrew those whom he could from William and drew them to Robert—many great and powerful men among both the **Normans** and the **English**, and quite a few of both.

### BOOK III.

...reigning. While William <note>William Rufus, reigned 1087–1100.</note> was reigning, a thick darkness had overshadowed the whole kingdom with a dense fog. And lest anything should seem to be missing from such great joy, as soon as he <note>Henry I, the younger brother of William Rufus.</note> took up the governance of the kingdom, Anselm was recalled from exile in the very first stages of the reign, and he was restored to his own see <note>The Archbishopric of Canterbury.</note> with the honor due to a man of such great reverence. For that reason, as if in a competition with the sounding applause of the common people, on the fourth day after the death of his brother, he was crowned in the highest dignity as King at London. 

The reason for such great haste was this: namely, that flying rumor had already filled the ears of all everywhere that his brother Robert, returning from the **Jerusalem expedition** <note>The First Crusade (1096–1099).</note> after completing God’s business, was now on the verge of arriving with a gathered army. Nor did the rumor flying about everywhere completely deceive them. For Robert, returning immediately from the East, received the principality of Normandy with no one resisting—indeed, with every favor. 

When the rumor of this matter spread, almost all the nobles deserted King Henry and, as oath-breakers and deserters, surrendering themselves to Robert, they swore their oaths of allegiance to him. Some did this for no apparent reasons; others for slight excuses begged from wherever they could find them—specifically, because the King would not give them those lands which they wanted to have according to their own whim. But Robert fitz Hamon, and Richard de Reviers, and Roger Bigot, and Robert, Count of Meulan, remained steadfast in their loyalty. All the others either secretly sent messages on behalf of Robert so that he might become king, or openly insulted the King by calling him "Godric" and the Queen "Godriva" <note>original: *Godricum, Godricam*; these were common Anglo-Saxon names used mockingly by the Norman barons to ridicule Henry I and his wife, Matilda, for their English sympathies and customs.</note>.

In the second year of King Henry's reign, his brother Robert, having crossed the sea with a massive fleet, entered England; there he deployed and spread out his forces. # THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

Of the King <note>This likely refers to Theobald, Count of Blois, the elder brother of Stephen, who was a potential claimant to the English throne.</note>, when he was already on the verge of his journey, prepared to cross over into England so that he might distinguish himself with the royal crown by right of hereditary succession; having heard and found it to be true that his aforementioned brother—namely, Stephen—had already crossed over with the same intention, he ceased from his undertaking. His sons (Henry the Young King, Richard the Lionheart, Geoffrey, and John) famously rebelled against him in 1173–1174.</note> On this point, some think the word should be "of the one reigning" <note>original: *regentis*</note> rather than "of the roaring one" <note>original: *rugientis*</note>—meaning simply "of the king"—but they pay too little attention to how much more fittingly and expressively it is said that the "roaring cubs" shall awaken, following the metaphor and the natural properties of the Lion.

For those who have written on the natures of animals and beasts <note>A reference to medieval Bestiaries, which combined natural history with moral lessons.</note> say that when a lioness has given birth to her offspring, the little cubs sleep for three days as if they were dead. On the third day, however, they are roused and wake up at the horrific roar and terrifying bellowing of their parent; and when they have grown, they learn to seize prey and devour men, just as the prophetic word speaks. In this way, while these "cubs" <note>The princes.</note> were in their infancy and childhood, they behaved innocently and without any malice according to their age—much like those who sleep—but now in their youth, as if on the third day, they have awakened at the bellowing and horrific roar of their parent. Under their tutors and guardians, they are now learning to seize prey and devour men. And this is what he means when he says: *The cubs of the roaring one shall awaken, and, setting aside the forests, they shall hunt within the walls of the cities,* not by shooting arrows at wild beasts, but by destroying men.

...we must, however, understand that sixth person who is to reign in England after those [first] four, and another, the fifth—whoever he may be, that is, whether he is their brother or not—of whom it is said that he will overthrow the walls of Ireland <note>original: *Hyberniæ*</note>, cut down the forests, and change diverse portions into a plain. By "wandering affections," he signifies either the flighty inconstancy of the man's mind, or the incontinent and petulant lust of his body regarding various and wandering sexual unions. Yet these vices, contracted in the first flower of youth with a youthful heat, the prophecy says he will redeem in his final days with the most ample virtues and a religious and pious zeal toward God and the Churches of God. ...wishing to perform penance for his flesh, and for this reason undertaking a laborious journey by land and sea, first to Pope Innocent, traveling all the way to Rome, and secondly to Eugenius, who was the fourth Pope after Innocent; on that very journey, at Clairvaux <note>original: *claram vallem*; the famous Cistercian abbey in France</note>, he was seized by a fever and, in the place and at the time which he had long before chosen and foretold, he happily fell asleep in the Lord <note>A traditional phrase meaning he died a peaceful, Christian death.</note>. *He shall clothe two cities with two palliums, and shall give virginal gifts to virgins.* This means he will build suitable monastic dwellings for holy virgins, or he will enlarge those already built with worthy gifts and possessions. <term>Pallium</term> <note>A circular band of white wool worn by archbishops, symbolizing their authority and connection to the Pope; here it refers to the status of the cities.</note> *He shall thereby earn the favor of the Thunderer, and shall be placed among the blessed.* <note>The "Thunderer" (original: *tonantis*) is a poetic, classical title for God.</note> But not all sons resemble their fathers; instead, by a turn of fate, the worst sometimes arise from the best parents, and occasionally good ones from wicked fathers. Thus, from the aforementioned King—who, abounding in such illustrious virtues, will be deemed worthy to be placed among the blessed—there shall be born a son entirely unlike his father’s goodness. Whence it follows: *From him shall go forth a Lynx penetrating all things, who shall threaten the ruin of his own people.* The Lynx is an animal born from a wolf and a dog. For this reason, it is called a "Lynx" because it is joined to the genus of wolves. In Greek <note>original: *Graece*</note>, a wolf is called *Lykos* <note>original: *Λύκος*</note>. It is, moreover, of varied color, namely with a spotted hide. <margin>Virgil, *Aeneid* Book 1.</margin> Whence the poet says: *girded with a quiver and the hide of a spotted Lynx.* Furthermore, this word "Lynx" is used for both the male and female—that is, a "stag-wolf" or "she-stag-wolf"—of a common gender just like "dog," "pig," and other such words. Hence some doubt whether a man or a woman—that is, a daughter or a son—is designated by the name of the lynx...

# THE PROPHECY OF MERLIN

...and of the Normans, who now inhabit it [the island], not as rightful heirs and citizens, but as foreign invaders. It follows: *A snowy old man also, upon a snowy horse, shall divert the river of Periron, and with a white wand he shall measure out a mill upon it.*

Just as those who besiege cities or castles are accustomed to divert, with immense labor, the rivers flowing into them—directing them elsewhere from their course—so that the abundance of water is taken away from the besieged townsfolk and they may be more easily captured unless they surrender; so shall this **snowy old man** do at **Periron** <note>original: *Perironis*. Moreover, he calls him a "snowy old man," either literally because of his age and his venerable white hair, or figuratively because of his honorable and excellent character, according to that scripture:

This famous passage from Geoffrey of Monmouth identifies Arthur as the "Boar of Cornwall" (Aper Cornubiae) who saves Britain.</note> 

He is truly a man worthy that no "old wives' tales" should lie about him, but rather that true histories should speak of him with truth and worthy praise. For he restored his own nation, which had been trampled by foreigners, to its former dignity, and he drove the treacherous invaders from the borders of the fatherland. He reformed the religious worship, which had been almost destroyed in cities, villages, and towns; he restored the Churches destroyed or ruined by the pagan people, and in them he ordained pastors and bishops with the duties of clerics, just as the dignity of the places required, with a devoted zeal for religion. 

Not only this, but he was so devoted toward the blessed Mother of God, Mary, that he even had her image painted on his shield, and he had placed so much confidence in her that in all his necessities and dangers, he constantly invoked her with all the innermost feelings of his heart. Nor was he frustrated in his hope. Indeed, with her helping and protecting him in all his battles, remaining invincible against the enemies of the faith, he continually brought back glorious triumphs over his adversaries. 

Therefore, the Britons can by no means be persuaded to believe that this man of such great fame and such great glory is dead—especially since in no annals can it be found written exactly where he either died or was buried.

In this battle, the traitor fell, and Arthur himself, being mortally wounded, had himself carried to the Isle of Avalon to have his wounds cared for. This was in the year of our Lord’s incarnation 541. He left the governance of the kingdom to his kinsman Constantine, the son of Cador, Duke of Cornwall. Because, therefore, neither this history nor any other speaks of the death of so great a King, for no reason, as has been said...

# PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

...[hardly] can the Britons be led to believe in his death; instead, all—or nearly all—that nation believe that he still hides and lives on the **Isle of Avalon**, <note>original: "Insula Auallonis." ### BOOK III.

...will receive companionship. Then there will be a slaughter of foreigners, then rivers will flow with blood. Then the **Armorican** <note>original: "Armorici." What this says is this: in the time of **Cadwaladr**, <note>original: "Cadualadri." When, however, that deadly plague of mortality and famine had ceased through God's mercy, and the king was preparing to sail back to his homeland with a great fleet and a multitude of Armoricans, he was ordered by an **angelic warning** to desist from his undertaking. Concerning him, the prophet further adds: *For he shall cut down all the greater oaks, but to the smaller ones he shall grant protection.* What he says has this meaning: he will either deprive the powerful and those placed in high positions of the joy of temporal life by killing them, or, by stripping away their substance, he will cut them off from their own possessions. A certain person said something similar in praise of the Romans: *To spare the conquered and wear down the proud in war.* <note>original: "Parcere subiectis, & debellare superbos." Furthermore, in that which he says—*he shall cut down the greater things, but to the smaller ones he shall grant protection*—he clearly declares that he is speaking not of a beastly boar, but of a "human boar." Otherwise, it is known to be entirely against the nature and habit of boars to cut down the greater oaks and larger trees while sparing the smaller ones; for boars, on the contrary, destroy the smaller and tender shrubs, while not even touching the larger ones.

<margin>Exodus 5, verse 21</margin>
> You have made your scent to stink <note>original: "Fætere fecistis odorem vestrum." A biblical metaphor for making oneself loathsome or hated.</note> before Pharaoh and his servants,
they say to them. But in contrast, the divine word says this of King Josiah, who was surely the best of kings and beloved by God:
<margin>Ecclesiasticus, chapter 49, verse 1</margin>
> The memory of Josiah is like a blending of incense, made by the work of a perfumer <note>original: "pigmentarij." In the medieval context, this refers to an apothecary or one who prepares spiced wines and perfumes.</note>. In every mouth, his memory will be tasted like honey, and like music at a banquet of wine.

The goat of the Castle of Venus <note>The "Castle of Venus" is a metaphorical name for the king's court or private chambers, characterized by lust.</note> follows, having golden horns. There is another meaning in these golden horns and silver beard, and indeed a clear enough one: that, contenting ourselves with a simple interpretation, we may understand by these words that this goat will possess a great abundance of gold and silver. This is what the prophet wished to signify through the golden horns and silver beard, so that he might preserve the metaphor of the goat, which possesses both horns and a beard. 

And it should be noted what great distinction of words he used, so that he did not speak of a golden beard and silver horns, but conversely, golden horns and a silver beard. Why so? Surely because the strength of the animal is greater in the horns, and its confidence is greater there, since it uses them as weapons, more so than in its beard. And for that reason, its own horns are more beloved by the animal than its beard. > Humble fortune once kept the Latin women chaste, and did not allow their tiny homes to be touched by vice; labor, short periods of sleep, and hands hardened and worn by the dark wool <note>original: "vellere Fusco." ### BOOK VI.

A 6

...are celebrated; that is, so great will be your luxury in these things, and they will pull such long <term>trains</term> <note>original: "syrmata." A *syrma* was a long, trailing robe worn by tragic actors in antiquity, which became a symbol of excessive female fashion.</note> behind them—which are commonly called "tails"—that they are rightly compared to **Basilisk** serpents. This is because from their middle part—that is, the upper part—they walk upright, but the middle part—namely the rear and lower section—crawls; they do not so much walk as they are dragged. 

Hence, women of this kind, walking with the proudest arrogance, have need of support at their sides, whether from their little maids or from their attendants and household slaves, being hampered as they are by such a great overflow of clothing. And this is what the prophecy means when it says: *Women shall become serpents in their gait, and all their steps are celebrated in pride*; that is, they will be surrounded by a proud and famous procession. 

Hence, noting the luxury of women regarding such a dragging of trains, the poet says among other things: *They walk sweeping the earth with a long train.* <note>original: "Incedunt longo verrentes Syrmate terram."</note> For among Roman and Italian women, this superfluous and proud luxury of trains was so famous from ancient times that it could never be restrained for long, either by the indignation of husbands or even by the excommunication of bishops. The bishops, of course, detested the arrogance of their pride, while the husbands complained of the excessive expense of the clothes; the "little women," however, ignored both with a hardened brow. 

Hence their own poet—I speak of **Juvenal**—in his **Sixth Satire**, after he had spoken at length with sharp and vehement declamation concerning the immodesty of women, did not remain silent about this point either, 

<margin>Juvenal, Satire 6.</margin>
saying: *The extravagant woman does not feel her wealth perishing,*

### PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

...*to be wounded by Cupid's arrows*. The **Camps of Venus** are named by <term>antiphrasis</term> <note>original: "Antiphrasim" — a rhetorical figure of speech where a word is used in a sense opposite to its actual meaning; for example, calling a dwarf a "giant."</note>, for the reason that in those places life is not lived chastely at all. For "camps" <note>original: "Castra"</note> are so named from "chastity" <note>original: "castitate"</note>, because in them soldiers are meant to live chastely, as if they were <term>eunuchs</term> <note>original: "castrati" — the author is using a common medieval false etymology to link military discipline with sexual abstinence.</note>. 

And it should be noted what the prophecy says: *the camps of Venus shall be renewed*. For when good and excellent princes are reigning, fornications and adulteries are restrained by severe laws, and thus the "Camps of Venus" seem to be dismantled and Cupid’s arrows blunted. However, under a most wicked prince—who, in the things he permits for himself, thinks he must also permit for others so that he does not appear to be the only villain among them—the reins of shamelessness are loosened. Then, the **Camps of Venus** appear to be "renewed," and the arrows of lust are sharpened and polished.

Such was the case with the famous **Semiramis**, once Queen of the Assyrians. Although she had subjugated nearly half the world to her empire by force of arms—from Ethiopia even to the furthest reaches of India—she perished through an illicit and incestuous love for her own son. When her unrestrained madness finally dragged him, unwilling and weeping, to her bed, she sought to excuse or diminish the shame of her unspeakable crime, which was unheard of in all previous times. She promulgated a law for all the nations she ruled, decreeing that mothers might be joined to their sons, and sons to their mothers, in lawful marriage. The Medes, Persians, Derbians, Bactrians, Hyrcanians, and all those barbarian peoples—including many of the Indians—accepted this as law and turned it into custom and habit. It remained so for many centuries, until the preaching—

Enflamed and captured by love for her, two Kings will engage in a duel—either fighting between themselves or each committing two others (that is, one for each side) to the fight. ...in the **Tower of London** <note>original: "turrim Londoniarum"</note> a tree shall be born, which, content with only three branches, shall overshadow the entire surface of the Island with the breadth of its leaves. Against this, **Boreas** <note>original: "Boreas"; the personification of the North Wind</note> shall come, and with his hostile blast shall snatch away the third branch. I have set down many things at once, the meaning of which, as it seems to me, is this. **London** <note>original: "Londonia"</note> is a city which **Brutus** <note>Brutus of Troy, the legendary first King of the Britons who was said to have founded the city as "New Troy."</note>, the first King of the Britons, built upon the **River Thames** <note>original: "Tamesem fluuium"</note> as the first of all cities in the island; he willed it to be the head of the kingdom and the **Metropolis** <note>In this context, the "mother city" or capital of the realm.</note>. Therefore, the Tower of London signifies the prominence of that kingdom. 

In the Tower of London, then—either according to the <term>literal sense</term> <note>The historical or plain meaning of the words.</note> or according to the <term>allegorical sense</term> <note>The symbolic or hidden spiritual meaning.</note>—a tree shall be born, which, content with only three branches, shall overshadow the entire surface of the Island with the breadth of its leaves. This means that in the Tower of London, according to both senses, a king shall be born who will have only three sons; these sons, dividing the island into three parts for themselves, will occupy the entire face of the kingdom with their domains. 

Then **Boreas** shall come—that is, some prince from the northern part of the island—who will snatch away one of the three, which is to say, he will kill him, and the two remaining sons will obtain his land. Something similar occurred among the sons of **Brutus**. For when Brutus died, his "three branches"—that is, his three sons, youths of renowned integrity—divided the kingdom among themselves,

# THE PROPHECY OF MERLIN

...a planet <note>original: "neta", likely part of "planeta"</note> hot and dry, as is, for example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, Mars when the sun is in the same sign. From such a conjunction, the heat and dryness of summer is doubled—summer itself being naturally hot and dry—whereby such great fervor descends upon the lands that sometimes the earth is ignited and burns from this cause. Many in our own days claim to have seen this happen, especially in marshes and swamplands <note>original: "marescis & paludum locis"</note> where, once all the moisture of the waters has been swallowed and exhausted by the heat of the sun, the earth remains parched and thirsty, gaping open with cracks. Because the air is set on fire and made glowing by the excessive heat of the sun, it easily enters and penetrates through its extreme thinness. Finding that earth to be cavernous, like a sponge, the air introduces itself, and by its own motion and heating, it sets the earth on fire and makes it burn. It could therefore happen in those days that the heat of summer becomes so great that the earth, ignited in the aforementioned manner, also sets fire to the nearby and neighboring wood of the groves so that they burn. This will certainly be a greater miracle to the people of that time because it will seem unusual and, until then, unheard of. And this is what he means when he says: *In those days oaks shall burn throughout the groves,* and he adds, *and on the branches of linden trees acorns shall grow.* This too can happen according to the laws of nature, although perhaps it has never occurred. For just as the shoots of different trees—which the common people call grafts <note>term: "graphias"; refers to the process of grafting a scion from one tree onto the stock of another.</note>—when grafted into trees of another kind, they unite and grow and bring forth fruit of their own kind; so I do not see why, in a similar way, the shoots of oaks grafted onto the trunks <note>original: "mirinicis vel stipitibus"</note> or stems of other trees...

### BOOK IV.

...by the course of its channel, it withdraws elsewhere, toward other regions.

Furthermore, the mouths of the sea are in some cases natural, and in others artificial—that is, made by human labor and industry, as we have learned was done in many places in ancient times. To demonstrate what we are saying with an example: the Seine <note>original: "Sequana"</note> is a river that preserves both its course and its name all the way to the Ocean. But before it reaches there, it receives into itself many rivers of lesser fame and name, and by receiving them, it takes away their own names. If that natural flow of these rivers into the Seine were removed by some labor or work, so that they were diverted through other channels to that sea, it would surely have more mouths than it has now. 

Thus, perhaps, it will happen to the Severn Sea. Now, the Severn Sea <note>original: "Sabrinum æquori"</note> is a certain gulf of the Ocean which encloses Wales <note>original: "VValliam"</note> and in certain places divides it from Loegria, which is now called England, as was stated above. The Severn Sea is named after the River Severn <note>original: "Sabrino fluuio"</note>, which flows into it. Furthermore, the name "Sabrina" comes from Habren <note>original: "Abren"</note>, the daughter of Locrinus, the son of Brutus <note>The author refers to the foundation myth of Britain where Brutus of Troy is the first king. His three sons—Locrinus, Albanactus, and Camber—inherited England (Loegria), Scotland (Albania), and Wales (Cambria) respectively.</note>. For during the reign of Locrinus, after his father’s death, Humber, the King of the Huns, arrived in Albania—that is, Scotland—with a huge fleet. Having joined battle with Albanactus, the King of Albania, he killed him. When Locrinus heard this, he joined with Camber <note>original: "Cābro"</note> and went out to meet him to avenge his brother. Humber, however, turned to flight and reached a certain river into which he threw himself and died. For this reason, that river is called the Humber. He had snatched...

### BOOK IV.

...will appear to happen contrary to custom. This is the heat of which we spoke earlier, which will be so intense that the scorched earth will even catch fire and burn the nearby woods and the surrounding timber. Regarding this, it is said: *In those days the oaks throughout the groves shall burn.*

Furthermore, it is consistent with the laws of nature that from the excessive heat of waters, the volume of water diminishes—just as it does with urine—and the waters lose their natural power and become corrupted. From this corruption, the native fish die. For every corruption of nature turns into corruption for those who use or consume it. 

However, concerning what is said of the Usk alone—that *it shall boil for seven months*—one must not think that the other rivers of the island will not boil similarly. Since all these rivers are located under the same region of the sky, they are all equally subject to either cold or heat. Perhaps, however, the prophecy mentions only the Usk because, although the others will suffer an equal heat, the mortality of the fish will not be equal elsewhere, nor will there be a similar procreation of serpents from the dead fish <note>The text refers to the medieval belief in spontaneous generation, where decaying matter was thought to produce new, often "unclean" life forms like serpents.</note>.

It signifies, therefore, a deadly war to come in the island, and such a slaughter of men that twenty thousand of the citizens of London alone are to be killed, and the River Thames will overflow with the corpses of the dead and appear to be changed into blood. There follows: *The hooded ones <note>original: "Cucullati." This refers to monks, identified by their hoods or cowls.</note> shall be provoked to marriages, and their cry shall be heard in the mountains of the Alps.* Here, to tell the truth, I am torn between two choices, and I know not which to choose: namely, whether to remain silent or to speak what I feel. For shame commands silence, yet the order of the explanation I have undertaken does not allow me to be quiet. What then shall I do? To use the words of blessed Job: <margin>Job ch. 16, v. 6</margin> *If I speak, my grief does not rest; and if I remain silent, it will not depart from me.* <note>original: "Si locutus fuero, non quiescit dolor meus, & si tacuero, nō recedet à me."</note> Forgive a man who is both ashamed to speak and unable to keep silent. *The hooded ones shall be provoked to marriages, and their cry in the mountains...*

...[shall be heard in the] Alps. <note>original: "Alpium audietur." This concludes a sentence from the prophecy: "The cry of the hooded ones shall be heard in the mountains of the Alps."</note> Oh, what confusion! Oh, what shame!

# THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

<page-num>138</page-num>

<header>THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN</header>

Duty breeds friendship <note>original: "Officium parat amicitiam"; a common Latin proverb suggesting that performing one's service or duty leads to favor</note>. Nevertheless, no one who truly loves the sacred order will think that either Jerome or anyone else should be justly resented if—as a lover and praiser of that order—he reproaches and laments its corruption and the vices which unruly men have brought into the order through the "guardianship" of the order, which is to say, through the negligence of the Abbots. For indeed, many things are done in the order which are not *of* the order. For how can those things be thought to belong to the order which are done against the order? Indeed, no order admits anything disorderly. Otherwise, an order is no longer an order. 

But if there are those who are unreasonably indignant against those who are justly moved by the disorders committed in the order against the order—and who reproach these things out of love for the brotherhood and the order itself—they reveal themselves as men who do not truly love the order; for they do not wish its destruction and ruins to be mourned and lamented by the order’s true lovers. 

For now, through men indulging too much in the allurements of gluttony, that once-glorious order—which was the first in the Church, and from which the Church itself began among the Apostles—has now, I say, come to this, or rather collapsed to this point: that if any among them wish to be lovers and followers of sobriety, they are thought to be Manichaeans <note>Manichaeans were followers of a dualistic heresy known for extreme, sometimes performative asceticism; here, the term is used as a slur to mock monks who actually follow their vows of fasting</note>; frugality is called hypocrisy; thriftiness is labeled as greed; and silence is ascribed to rudeness. 

But on the contrary, these preachers of a "new Gospel" call gluttony <note>original: "gastrimargiam"; a Greek-derived technical term for "belly-madness" or excessive gluttony</note> "discretion," and they call talkativeness "affability"...

They call prodigality "liberty," and loud laughter and derision they call "refined urbanity" and "courtly manners." They call the lavish pride of horses "honor," and the costly care of clothes "cleanliness." Who would have believed the holy order, at its beginning, would fall into such dissolution and laziness?
