# EXPLANATIONS
## OF THE PROPHECY OF MERLIN
->By Ambrosius the Briton,<-
### BOOK FIVE.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring ornate scrollwork and foliage within a square frame.</image-desc> Three fountains shall burst forth in the city of Winchester <note>original: "VVintonia"</note>, whose streams shall divide the island into three portions. He who drinks of one shall enjoy a longer life, nor shall he be burdened by any oncoming sickness. He who drinks of the second shall perish in unending hunger, and upon his face shall sit paleness and horror. He who drinks of the third shall be endangered by sudden death, nor shall his body be able to enter a grave. Those wishing to avoid such excessive gluttony <note>original: "ingluuiem," referring to the destructive consumption or the overwhelming nature of the fountains</note> will strive to hide it with various coverings. Whatever mass is thrown over it, therefore, shall take the form of another body. For earth shall be turned into stones, stones into wood, wood into ashes, and ash into water, if they are thrown over it. 

In addition to these things, from the city of Canute’s Wood <note>original: "Canuti nemoris," historically associated with the region of Southampton or the New Forest</note>, a maiden shall be brought to light to provide a healing cure. Once she has mastered all the arts, with her breath alone she shall dry up the harmful fountains. Thereafter, when she has refreshed herself with wholesome liquid, she shall carry in her right hand the Forest of Caledon <note>The legendary Caledonian Forest in Scotland, often cited as Merlin's retreat</note>, and in her left hand the ramparts of the walls of London. Wherever she walks, she shall leave sulfurous steps which shall burn with a double flame. That smoke shall rouse the Ruthenians <note>original: "Ruthenos," a term usually referring to the people of Rus/Eastern Europe, but used here in a symbolic prophetic sense for distant or foreign peoples</note> and shall prepare food beneath the sea. She herself shall flow with pitiable tears and fill the island with a horrid cry.

# BOOK V.

...[it] will. A stag of ten branches shall slay her, four of which shall bear golden diadem-crowns. The remaining six, however, shall be turned into the horns of oxen, which shall move the three islands of Britain with a dreadful sound.

Winchester <note>original: "Vintonia"</note> is one of the most noble cities of Britain, which Hudibras, King of the Britons, founded while Rehoboam <note>original: "Roboam"</note>, the son of Solomon, was reigning in Judea. This Hudibras was the eighth descendant from Brutus <note>The legendary Trojan founder of Britain according to medieval myth</note>.

*Therefore, in this city of Winchester, three fountains shall burst forth in the days of the ass of wickedness, whose streams shall divide the island into three portions. He who drinks of one, it says, shall enjoy a longer life, nor shall he be burdened by any oncoming sickness. He who drinks of the second shall suffer from unending hunger, and upon his face shall sit paleness and horror. He who drinks of the third shall be endangered by sudden death, nor shall his body be able to enter a grave.*

These words, which seem to be shrouded in great obscurities and are far too hidden, must first be carefully and gradually considered and examined, to see whether something of this sort could happen in nature, according to the literal sound of the words and the nature of springs or waters. Then, if no literal explanation <note>original: "exitus," literally an 'exit' or solution to the puzzle</note> can be found for us, we must flee to allegorical and mystical understandings, in whose coverings the entire surface of this book is known to be hidden. And indeed, histories—not only of the pagans <note>original: "gentilium"</note> but also our own—report marvelous and almost incredible things about the natures and diversity of fountains or waters; if I wished to bring all of these forward, time would fail me before the examples would.

Yet I shall bring forward a few examples from among many. Saint Augustine <note>A reference to Book 21 of *The City of God*, where Augustine lists natural marvels to prove that God can perform miracles that seem to defy the laws of nature</note> reports that there is a fountain in Epirus <note>A region in northwestern Greece</note> in which, if you submerge burning torches, they are extinguished according to the nature of all springs and waters. If, however, they are extinguished and then submerged, they are immediately relighted against the nature of all springs and waters. He also speaks of another fountain, which is among the distant Garamantes <note>An ancient tribal civilization located in the Saharan region of modern-day Libya</note>, which is so cold by day that it cannot be drunk, and so hot at night that it cannot be touched. Who would not be stunned and marvel at both these things, especially since that land lies under the most burning region of the sky, being next to and neighboring the Torrid Zone <note>In ancient geography, the area of the Earth too hot for human habitation; here it refers to the tropics</note>? Indeed, the native people—the Garamantes—are said to curse the creator of the sun on account of the sun's intolerable heat. Augustine also claims there is a fountain in the region of Alisma which is otherwise quiet when there is silence; but if flutes should sound above it or near it, it immediately rises up exultantly at the song and leaps into the air, as if delighted and enticed by the vocal sweetness.

In Dacia <note>original: "Datia"; an ancient region in Central/Eastern Europe</note> there is a fountain, as those who have seen and proven it tell us—men who are reverend and holy—into which if you submerge a cloth, it is immediately turned to stone. So much so that if you do not wish to submerge the whole thing, only the part submerged is converted into stone, while the rest remains a cloth as it was before.

In Sardinia there is a fountain that reveals thefts; for when someone who is accused of theft is compelled to drink from it for the sake of knowing the truth, if they are guilty, they are blinded as soon as they have drunk. Because this has often...

There is yet another on the same island which, if seen by anyone, immediately causes the most violent rains to pour down from the heavens; these rains do not agree to cease until a holy offering has been sacrificed to God. There is another which, when it is seen by a healthy man <note>original: *homine sanatiuo*</note> who is destined to live for a long time in safety, rises up as if joyful, leaping and applauding. There is also water there in which, if anyone washes their body, they become leprous.

There is also a certain pool there in which pieces of wood, once thrown in and left, are found after seven years to have turned into stone. And as it seems to pertain more closely to the matter we have at hand, there is a certain lake in Sicily <note>original: *Sicilia*</note> in which there is a shelf <note>original: *ara*, literally "altar," here referring to a raised stone formation</note> that separates the shallow waters from the deep. Similarly, in Ireland <note>original: *Hybernia*</note> there are two fountains situated a short distance from one another, yet differing from each other with such great disparity that a drink from one kills the drinker, while the other preserves life, being harmless and healthful. ### BOOK V.

That fountains should break out from the earth from subterranean water passages, which no previous age has seen, is not a new thing, since many thousands of men in many places on earth testify to having frequently seen such things in great numbers. Let these things we have said suffice for the literal sense of the text.

However, I do not doubt that beneath this literal envelope <note>original: *literali inuolucro*; a medieval term for the "wrapping" or outer layer of a story that conceals a deeper allegorical truth</note>, a far higher understanding is enfolded. That "waters" in the Scriptures designate people, few doubt, according to that [saying]: <margin>Isaiah 32:20</margin> *Blessed is he who sows upon all waters, sending in the foot of the ox and the donkey.*

Indeed, anyone—unless perhaps the most simple-minded <note>original: *pientissimus*; literally "most pious," but here implying one who is too uncritical or literal-minded</note>—would easily notice that according to the literal sound <note>original: *sibilum*, literally "hissing" or "whistling," referring to the superficial sound of the words</note> of the letter, this would be most false. For there are many waters, rivers, and torrents that very frequently overflow the boundaries and limits of their channels, so that they drown and kill the crops and harvests, rendering the land marshy and sterile. Therefore, those who have sown in such conditions, being frustrated in their expectation of fruit, would not consider themselves blessed in this regard, but rather unhappy, as they have entirely lost both their labor and their expense.

Furthermore, in what the verse says—"sending in the foot of the ox and the donkey"—it seems to speak against the edict of the Law <note>Refers to the Mosaic Law in Deuteronomy 22:10, which forbids yoking an ox and a donkey together for plowing</note>, since the Law prohibits plowing with an ox and a donkey together. Because, therefore, what is said cannot stand according to the outward sound of the letter—*Blessed is he who sows upon all waters, sending in the foot of the ox and the donkey*—we must seek another understanding in these words of wisdom: one that is true, probable, and worthy of the very wisdom of God. For there are certain other waters, about which in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>...

...of God, just as the wisdom of God himself has bestowed, "Blessed," you say, "is he who sows upon all waters." <note>original: "beatus, inquies, qui seminat super omnes aquas"; a reference to Isaiah 32:20, interpreted here as spreading divine truth among many nations.</note> For God shall see what comes of the harvest of seeds; for nothing is lost to the sower, nor is there reason to fear being cheated of his due reward, as the Apostle says: *Each one shall receive a reward according to his own labor.* <note>original: "Unusquisque mercedem accipiet secundum suum laborem"; quoting the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 3:8.</note> For he is to be gifted with that blessedness by which the faithful and wise servant—whom the Lord has set over his household—gives them their measure of wheat in due season. <note>A reference to the parable in Matthew 24:45, where "wheat" represents spiritual nourishment or teaching.</note> Wherefore another of the saints dares to say: *Those who are learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who have instructed many in righteousness, like stars for all eternity.* <note>Quoting Daniel 12:3.</note> Therefore the wisdom of God also advises, saying: *Cast your bread upon the passing waters, for after a long time you shall find it.* <note>Quoting Ecclesiastes 11:1.</note>

Therefore, the faithful and prudent steward, whom the Lord has set over his household to give them their food in due season, ought to give to the "passing waters"—that is, to mortal and fleeting men—the measure of wheat in the form of sevenfold and eightfold loaves. This means he must instruct the people of God with the pages of both Testaments, so that he may be a scribe learned in the kingdom of God, like a merchant who brings forth from his treasure things new and old. For the new things harmonize with the old, and the old with the new. # THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

Locrinus, Camber, and Albanactus divided their father's kingdom into three portions, as I remember mentioning earlier. Locrinus, because he was the firstborn, received **Loëgria** <term>Loëgria</term> <note>The legendary name for the territory of England, derived from the name Locrinus.</note> along with the royal crown; Camber, however, received **Cambria**, which is now called <term>Wales</term>; and Albanactus received **Albania**, which they now call <term>Scotland</term>. In the same way, the grandsons of Locrinus—namely **Mempricius** and **Malim**, the sons of the late Madan—divided their father's kingdom into two parts between themselves. And because, as <term>Lucan</term> <note>Marcus Annaeus Lucanus (39–65 AD), a Roman poet known for his epic on the Roman Civil War; he is quoted here to emphasize the instability of shared power.</note> says: *“While the earth shall support the sea, and the air the earth; while the sun shall roll through its long labors, and the day does not follow the same signs in the sky, there is no trust between partners in kingship, and all power is impatient of a companion; do not trust any nations, nor need examples of fate be sought from afar: the walls first grew wet with a brother's blood, and the prize for such great madness was not then the earth and the sea; it was a small thing then—a meager refuge that set its masters against each other.”* <note>original: "dum terra fretum terramq3 leuabit aer, dum longi voluerit tytana labores... dominos commifit asilum." This quote from Lucan's 'Pharsalia' (I, 92-97) refers to the murder of Remus by his brother Romulus at the founding of Rome.</note>

A discord arose between the brothers over the kingdom. **Mempricius**, calling **Malim** to a meeting under the guise of negotiating for peace, killed him as a wicked murderer of his own kin and a traitor among the negotiators. But he did not go unpunished. For one day, while he was out hunting, he withdrew from his companions into a certain valley where, surrounded by a pack of rabid wolves, he paid the just penalty to his brother’s ghost, being most miserably devoured by the wolves. This occurred at the time when **Saul** was reigning in Judea. Later on, the cousins **Cunedagius** and **Marganus**, having shared the same kingdom, began to fight each other for the throne, and eventually Cunedagius killed Marganus in the province of Cambria.

*Three fountains shall break forth in the City of Winchester, and the rivulets shall cut the Island into three portions.*

This means, as we have said, that infants will be born in the aforementioned city <term>Winchester</term> <note>original: "Wintonia". Truly, they shall stand apart from one another with a great dissimilarity of both character and actions, and with much diversity. And indeed, earth can be turned into stones by physical reasoning <term>physica ratione</term>, for stones are the **bones of the earth**. Similarly, through old age, wood demolished by rot and corrupted will be converted into ash—that is, into dust. For dust is sometimes called ash, as in the scripture: *Remember that you are ash, and to ash you shall return*, <note>A reference to the Latin Vulgate, Genesis 3:19: "pulvis es et in pulverem reverteris." Furthermore, no natural reason teaches that stones can be converted into wood, or ashes into water. Therefore, it is a metaphorical and figurative way of speaking when he says: *Wishing to avoid such great filth, they will strive to hide it with various coverings. Whatever mass is placed upon it, therefore, will take the form of another body. For if they are cast upon it, earth will turn into stones, stones into wood, wood into ashes, and ash into water.* The interpretation of these words, as I have shown, is as follows: In whatever way they strive to block the lethal channels of the fountains—namely the second and the third—it will result in the opposite, just as if earth cast upon them were converted into stones, stones into wood, wood into ashes, and ash into water.

<margin>Boethius, *On the Consolation of Philosophy*</margin>

Our assertion is also supported by Boethius, in his book *On the Consolation of Philosophy*: where he speaks of that most famous sorceress, Circe, and how she changed the companions of Ulysses into beasts. He notes that although they appeared to have lost their human form, they nevertheless retained their human reason and mind intact. For he says:

> The East wind drove the wandering ships of the Neritian leader <note>original: "Næritii ducis"; a reference to Ulysses/Odysseus, whose home island of Ithaca was near Mount Neritos</note> over the sea to the island where the beautiful Goddess resides. Born from the seed of the Sun <note>original: "solis edita semine"; Circe was the daughter of the sun god Helios</note>, she mixes for her guests cups touched by harmful spells, which her hand—powerful in herbs—transforms in various ways. This man is covered by the face of a boar; that one becomes a Marmaric <note>North African</note> lion, growing with tooth and claw. This one, recently added to the wolves, howls just as he prepares to weep. Another, like an Indian tiger, walks tamely through the house. But although they suffered various evils, the winged god of Arcadia <note>original: "Numen Arcadis alitis"; refers to Mercury (Hermes), who gave Ulysses a magical herb to resist Circe's magic</note>, pitying the besieged leader, broke the guest's curse. Yet the rowers had already swallowed the evil potions from the cup. Now as swine they had turned to acorns for their food. Nothing remains whole, for their voices and bodies are lost; only the mind remains stable, groaning over the monstrous forms it endures. Oh, hand too light! Herbs are not so potent. Though they may have power over the limbs, they cannot change the heart. Within is the vigor of men, stored in a hidden citadel. Powerful poisons cannot strip a man of himself—those dreadful things that penetrate deep within.

### BOOK V.

...to spiritual men, and those who are confirmed in all things by the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, they are in no way able to mock with such a phantom <note>original: "fantasmate"; a term for a demonic illusion or hallucination that affects the senses without changing the underlying substance of a person or thing</note>. They act in such a way as to make those things which do not exist appear as if they were real, as many examples prove, which any studious and diligent reader will easily find at hand in the holy scriptures. 

For instance, when Simon Magus <note>Simon Magus was a biblical figure (Acts 8) often depicted in early Christian tradition as a sorcerer who used magic to rival the miracles of the Apostles</note> had imprinted his own likeness upon Faustinianus by using certain magical juices with which he had smeared the man's face, Faustinianus returned to his sons—namely Clement, Faustus, and Faustinus. They indeed recognized their father's voice, but they were terrified by the face of Simon, as if it were the devil’s own, wailing and weeping at these new tricks of ghostly delusion <note>original: "fantasticae delusionis praestigias"</note> seen in their father. Peter, however, said that he saw nothing of Simon at all in the man, but both heard the voice of Faustinianus and saw his true face.

So it is also read in the *Lives of the Fathers* <note>original: "Vitis Patrum"; a famous collection of stories about the early Christian desert monks of Egypt</note>, that a certain man, lusting after his neighbor's wife and wishing to join her to himself in marriage if she should be sent away by her husband for any reason, spoke to a certain sorcerer <term>magus/maleficus: a practitioner of "maleficium" or harmful magic</term>, offering him much if he could accomplish this regarding the girl: namely, that her husband might find her company loathsome and thus cast her out. What more can be said? By the outward appearance of her body, the magician changed her into a mare, though her human mind and reason were retained. For three days and as many nights she lay in bed without food, rejecting all nourishment out of grief and confusion. Thus, she would neither eat bread like a human, nor hay like a beast of burden.

Disturbed by this, they began to bring water to extinguish the fire and throw it into the flames. Admonished by their noise, the blessed Benedict ran to them; observing that the fire was in the eyes of the disciples, but was not in his own, he first offered a prayer and then commanded them to sign their eyes <note>original: "oculos suos signarent"; this refers to making the Sign of the Cross over their eyes to break the demonic hallucination</note>, and thus they should drive away every phantom of the devil. They did, therefore, what he commanded, and immediately that which he himself had promised was fulfilled in them.

Such also was that Pythoness in the Acts of the Apostles, who provided so much profit to her masters through her fortune-telling. # THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

Truly, if the transformations of physical things, which through magical arts seem to occur in different bodies and various shapes, happen more in appearance than in truth—as the blessed Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), an influential theologian who wrote extensively on the nature of demons and miracles</note> asserts—then what shall we say of those incantations or songs that change bodies not only by sight and a ghostly appearance, but also vex them with certain spectral effigies? These the common people call *vultulos* <term>vultulos: small wax or clay figures (often called poppets) used in sympathetic magic to harm the person they represent</term>, or "voids" <term>inanulos: likely referring to hollow or insubstantial spectral forms, derived from the Latin "inanis" for empty</term>. By these means, they afflict people with long-lasting and incurable diseases, or even kill them. And what of those spells which exert such terrible power over the hearts of men that they cause them to go mad with lust and love for women or men, wasting away miserably? For example, we read in the life of the great Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great (c. 330–379 AD), a founding figure in Greek monasticism</note>: there was a certain senator named Proterius who intended to consecrate his daughter to God in a monastery for women. However, the envious enemy <note>original: "inuidens inimicus"; a common medieval reference to the Devil</note> inflamed one of his servants with love for the girl.

This servant, not daring to reveal his passion, approached a certain magician and opened up about what he was suffering, promising him much gold if he could enjoy the desired embraces through his help. ### BOOK V

We prefer the right hand over the left and hold it in greater affection. For thus Jacob—though his outward eyes were dimmed <note>original: "caligans," referring to Jacob's blindness in old age as described in Genesis.</note>, yet he saw inwardly through the spirit of prophecy—when Joseph had placed his sons before him, namely Manasseh at his father's right hand and Ephraim at the left, so that he might bless them, Jacob crossed his hands <note>original: "cancellatis manibus," literally "with hands formed like a lattice or cross."</note> and placed his left hand upon Manasseh but his right upon Ephraim.

<margin>Genesis 48</margin>

When Joseph saw this and took it ill, he said to his father: *“It is not fitting so, father, because this one is the firstborn; place your right hand upon his head.”* But Jacob refused, saying: *“I know, my son, I know. Indeed, he too shall become a people and be multiplied, but his younger brother shall be greater than he.”*

In this same way, the maiden shall carry the Forest of Calidon <note>The Forest of Calidon (Caledonia) refers to the wild, legendary woodlands of Scotland.</note> in her right hand, but the battlements of the walls of London in her left. However, because as the scripture says:

<margin>Jeremiah 13:23</margin>

*“Can the Ethiopian change his skin?”* <note>original: "Æthyops mutare pellem suam." A biblical proverb meaning that one's nature is fixed.</note> the healthy liquid she drinks will be of no use to her in casting off her wickedness. From this it follows: *Wherever she walks, she shall make sulfurous steps, which will smoke with a double flame.* 

Sulfur has a foul odor; thus, the hot springs and boiling waters that arise from sulfur for use in baths are stinking. This signifies that wherever this maiden proceeds, she makes foul steps and leaves behind filthy traces everywhere. *“Wherever she walks, she shall make sulfurous steps, which will smoke with a double flame,”* that is, from both of her domains, which the prophet signified through the Forest of Calidon and the battlements of the walls of London—one of which she shall carry in her right hand and the other in her left.

It follows: *“That smoke shall rouse the Ruthenians, and shall prepare food beneath the sea.”* The Ruthenians <note>original: "Rutheni." While this term often refers to people of Eastern Europe or Rodez in France, the author here explicitly identifies them with Flanders.</note> are of Flanders...

### PROPHETIES OF MERLIN

<margin>Lucan</margin>
About whom Lucan <note>Lucan was a Roman poet (39–65 AD) who wrote the *Pharsalia*, an epic about the Roman civil wars.</note> says: *“The fair-haired Rutheni are released from their long post.”* <note>original: "Soluuntur flaui longa statione Rutheni."</note> They are called Rutheni because of their reddish hair <note>original: "à rutilo crine."</note>. And so that you may know for certain that the Rutheni are the Flemish <note>The author identifies the ancient Gallic tribe of the Rutheni with the medieval people of Flanders.</note>, read in the history of the Britons how Julius Caesar, when Gaul had been conquered and subjected to the Romans, stood on the Ruthenian shore and saw Britain. The island is divided by a narrow strait between Wissant and Dover <note>original: "Wissant & Dorobellum." Wissant was a major port in the Middle Ages for crossing to England.</note>. He asked what island it was, and heard it was Britain. Therefore, *that sulfurous and foul smoke* will stir up the Rutheni and drive them to harass Britain with arms and war. When a naval conflict has begun on both sides, many will be submerged in the sea and become food for sea beasts. This is what the prophecy means when it says: *“That smoke shall stir the Rutheni and shall prepare food for those beneath the sea.”*

However, the fact that the Rutheni will gain the upper hand in that gamble of war, with the Britons trampled and defeated, is signaled by the pitiable tears of that maiden. She is the one who, with the smoke of her own sulfur, will stir the Rutheni against herself, to her own detriment and the destruction of her own people. For it follows: *“She shall be drenched in pitiable tears and shall fill the Island with a horrid cry.”* This means she will lament her own misfortune and that of her people with a womanly wailing. What end she is to suffer, and how she will pay the funeral dues <note>original: "inferias redditura," referring to the ancient Roman custom of offerings to the spirits of the dead.</note> for such a great slaughter of her own, the following book will show. ### BOOK SIX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' set within a square frame, featuring elaborate scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>*“A stag of ten branches will kill her, four of which shall wear golden crowns. The remaining six, however, will be turned into the horns of wild oxen <note>original: "bubalorum." While often translated as buffalo, in a medieval context this refers to the large, fierce wild oxen of Europe.</note>, which with a dreadful sound shall disturb the three islands of Britain, etc.”* By an elegant metaphor, a stag is brought forth to slay the sorceress, since—as those who have written on the natures of animals have handed down to us—it is the nature of stags to consume serpents and devour poisonous little beasts <note>This refers to a common medieval belief found in bestiaries that stags were the natural enemies of snakes, drawing them out of their holes with their breath to destroy them; thus the stag symbolizes a purifier or a righteous leader destroying evil.</note>. Furthermore, by the stag—who, by the power of his running, easily leaps over all thorny obstacles unharmed and reaches the high ridges of mountains—is symbolized some great and powerful man, about to undertake arduous and massive labors. This may be that prince of the Rutheni <note>The Flemish, as identified on the previous page.</note> whom the sulfurous smoke of the maiden shall stir up against Britain (as the preceding passages indicated), or perhaps some other man whom the literal text does not explicitly name. For the preceding lines state: *“Wherever she walks, she shall make sulfurous steps, which shall smoke with a double flame. That smoke shall stir the Rutheni, and shall prepare food for those beneath the sea; she herself shall be drenched in pitiable tears, and shall fill [the island] with a horrid cry—”*

For both in the prophet Zechariah, regarding the four horns which he saw, and in Daniel, regarding the four horns of the goat, the angel interprets these as four kingdoms. The remaining six, however, will be turned into the horns of wild oxen, which with a dreadful sound shall disturb the three islands of Britain.”* Regarding these words, a twofold inquiry occurs to me, both of which are likely and probable. For we can understand by the "ten branches" of this stag either ten principalities subject to his rule—four of which will be actual kingdoms, as hinted at by the golden crowns they wear—or perhaps ten children whom he will have. Of these children, four will be kings, either reigning simultaneously in different kingdoms, or succeeding one another in the same kingdom, just like those "four roaring sons" mentioned previously: *“The cubs of the roarer shall awaken, and leaving the forests behind, shall hunt within the walls of cities. ### BOOK VI.

*...from the fourth into the third, from the third into the second, the thumb shall be rotated in the oil.* <note>This likely refers to a ritual of anointing or a symbolic gesture mentioned at the very end of the previous page.</note> Thus, therefore, the four aforementioned branches shall succeed in the same kingdom and shall wear golden diadems, or, as has been said, they shall possess diverse kingdoms. But what of the six remaining? Hear what follows: *“But the six remaining shall be turned into the horns of wild oxen, which with a dreadful sound shall disturb the three islands of Britain.”*

By the "horns of wild oxen" <note>original: "cornua bubalina." In the medieval mind, the "bubalus" was a fierce, wild bovine of the forest.</note>, which clash with a horrid sound in wars and strike those hearing them with great terror, the prophet signifies that the six remaining branches of the aforementioned stag will be a source of great terror to many; and with great noise and tumult, they will disturb the three islands of Britain.

<margin>Island.</margin>
An "island" <note>original: "Insula."</note> is so called as if placed "in the brine" <note>original: "in salo." This is a traditional medieval etymology, deriving the word "insula" (island) from "in salo" (in the salt water/sea).</note>, that is, in the sea. From this, that which is surrounded on all sides by the sea is properly named an island. Nevertheless, the "three islands of Britain" in this context are called its three provinces: that is, <term>Scotland</term> <note>original: "Scotia," here referring to the northern part of the island (Albania).</note>, <term>Wales</term> <note>original: "Cambria."</note>, and <term>Cornwall</term> <note>original: "Cornubia."</note>, as the following points suggest; although two of them are not surrounded on every side by the circuit of the sea.

For in the beginning, when the island first began to be inhabited, these three provinces were divided among themselves by the sons of <term>Brutus</term> <note>The legendary Trojan founder of Britain.</note> and a certain Corineus, one of his fellow soldiers. For upon the death of Brutus—who [granted] Cornwall to Corineus while he still lived—Locrinus, his firstborn, obtained <term>Loegria</term> <note>The legendary name for England, named after Locrinus.</note> as his kingdom with the crown. His two brothers, however—namely Camber and Albanactus—possessed <term>Cambria</term> <note>Wales, named after Camber.</note> and <term>Albania</term> <note>Scotland, named after Albanactus.</note> respectively. Therefore, the three provinces—that is, Scotland, Wales, and Cornwall—shall be disturbed by the dreadful sound of the horns of wild oxen, having joined their forces for wars, to invade <term>Winchester</term> <note>original: "Wintoniam." In medieval prophecy, Winchester often represented a seat of royal power or a pivotal location for the fate of the kingdom.</note> and to de-

For Hamo <note>original: "Hamo." A legendary Roman leader said to have given his name to Southampton (Hamtun).</note>, a commander under Claudius Caesar, having been killed there by Arthur, King of the Britons, marked that very place with his own name. Therefore, we can more readily understand that the episcopal throne of Winchester must be transferred to this place in the time of the aforementioned necessity, along with the remaining people, both because of the fortification of the place itself and also because of its proximity. For it is not far distant from Winchester. *Come, Wales, and join Cornwall to your side, and say to Winchester: the earth shall swallow you. Transfer the shepherd’s seat* <note>The "shepherd's seat" refers to the <term>Episcopal See</term> or the official seat of the Bishop.</note> *to where the ships land, and let the other members follow the head.* Then he adds the reason why a city of such great nobility deservedly must be cut down and destroyed. For it follows: *For the day hastens on which the citizens shall perish for the crime of perjury. The whiteness of the wool has done harm, and the variety of their dye. Woe to the perjured nation, for because of it, famous cities shall fall.* 

This is the lamentation of the Prophet, mourning a noble city about to fall because of the perjury of its citizens. As for what he says: *The whiteness of the wool has done harm, and the variety of their dye*, you may agree with the literal meaning by a simple interpretation—that we can understand their pride, which is most often noted in the dyeing of clothes and various finery—or certainly there is a deeper meaning in these words, pertaining more to the fraud of perjury, which I must not keep silent. For the whiteness of sheep’s wool—and no one doubts that these are simple animals—signifies the simplicity and purity of the soul. This is, as it were, stained by dyes when it is changed from the simplicity and purity of nature into duplicity and deceit.

*...she will fly around Britain, and with a nocturnal cry she will call together the winged creatures, and associate every kind of bird with herself. <margin>The Heron</margin>
The heron <note>original: "Ardea"</note> is a bird that is always unlucky in omens. Its sound is truly horrendous, and by such a sound it announces horrible and unlucky things. Now, the heron is named, according to the etymology of its name, as if it were <term>ardua</term> <note>meaning "lofty" or "steep"</note>, because it seeks lofty heights. Indeed, being impatient of rain, when it senses that storms are imminent, it flies to the heights where it suffers no harm from the rains. 

Therefore, by the "heron" is designated some detestable tyrant who is about to attack lofty things and plan great deeds. With piratical fickleness, he will sail around the island for two years, and by breaking in with nocturnal infestations, he will "call together every kind of bird and associate them with himself"—that is, he will gather fickle men and wandering robbers who will rush into the cultivated lands of mortals and devour everything. From this plundering and depopulation, famine will follow, and a dire mortality will follow the famine. For just as famine follows devastation, so does mortality follow famine. 

But when such great calamity has ceased, the detestable bird will go to the valley of Galabes, which is in the borders of Wales <note>original: "Cambriæ"</note>, and will raise it into a high mountain—that is, into a high and lofty mound. On the peak of it, he will also "plant an oak," which is to say he will build a tower out of oak timbers.

But since, as the poet says: *There is no trust among partners in power, and all sovereignty will be impatient of a colleague* <note>original: "Nulla fides regni sociis, omnisq; potestas, Impatiens consortis erit" — quoting Lucan’s Pharsalia, which describes the instability of shared rule</note>; and *since the first walls grew wet with a brother’s blood* <note>original: "fraterno primi maduerunt sanguine muri" — a reference to Romulus killing Remus at the founding of Rome</note>, the Fox also will first kill his own mother. Having previewed these events to provide an understanding of what has been written, let us return to the sequence of the text. *The Fox*, it says, *shall devour his mother*, either by destroying her through a wicked and parricidal crime, or perhaps—as often happens with the difficulties of the maternal womb—simply by coming forth into the light. 

For even that Brutus, the first ruler of Britain, just as a certain diviner had predicted, killed both his father and his mother; but he killed his mother by being born, and his father by accident when he was fourteen years old, while he was hunting stags with him. For an arrow shot at a stag struck his father as he ran past on a swift horse, killing him instantly.

# BOOK VI.

->To feign foolishness in the right place is the highest wisdom.<- <note>original: "Stultitiam simulare loco, prudentia summa est" — a common Latin maxim</note>

The Fox, feigning a donkey-like foolishness and an undisciplined wickedness toward the Germans <note>original: "Germanos"</note> against the laws of nature, and pretending to be one of them—as if he were a portentous monster taken up against nature—will terrify them and drive them into Neustria <term>Neustria: A historical region in the northwest of the Frankish kingdom, often associated here with Normandy</term>. *But they will rouse against her a tusked boar <note>original: "aprum dentosum"</note>, and having returned by ship, they will join battle with the Fox.*

Here he clearly declares that the Wolf, the Bear, and the Boar will not be beasts, but men, because beasts are not typically carried in ships, but men. Nor will any Fox be an actual fox, but a man, because such great armies of men are not usually gathered or fought against a fox. *The Wolf and the Bear will therefore rouse the tusked boar against the Fox, their sister <note>While the characters represent men, the author refers to the Fox as "sister" because the Latin word "vulpes" is grammatically feminine</note>, and having returned by ship to the island, they will join battle with her. When she enters into the contest, she will pretend to be dead and move the Boar to pity. Soon he himself will approach the corpse, and while he stands over it, he will breathe into her eyes and face. But she, not forgetting her past trickery, will bite his left foot and tear it entirely from his body. Making a leap, she will also snatch away his right ear and tail, and hide within the caverns of the mountains.*

<margin>Solinus.</margin>
He pursues the established metaphor of the Fox in his usual manner and, with an elegant figure of words, suggests her cunning. One of these tricks is as Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Latin grammarian and compiler of "wonders" known for his descriptions of animal behavior</note> reports: that sometimes, to deceive birds, she lies on her back in the dust with a bloodied body as if killed by beasts. Seeing this, birds fly from all directions as if to a dead corpse, so they may tear her apart piece by piece and devour her, as if in revenge for the other living creatures which she herself has torn—

# THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

...used to tear apart and devour. Being not at all ignorant of the Fox's tricks, they do not dare to approach any closer until they have first confirmed the truth of its death. Therefore, they fly around the Fox and, as if with fear, they approach step-by-step, then immediately retreat, and approach again, panting with a keen scent into its face, wishing to find out for certain whether it lives or is a dead corpse. And they do this for so long until one of them, more reckless than the rest and more unfortunate, approaching too incautiously, is suddenly snatched by the fox, to be torn by its claws and devoured by its teeth.

So, therefore, this Fox of whom we speak is going to do exactly this; for when she enters the contest with her brothers and the tusked boar, and sees that she is unequal either in number or in strength, and sees that she must use guile rather than war: then, it says, *she will feign that she is dead, and will move the Boar to pity*. That is, *she will pretend that she is despairing in her affairs, as if lacking confidence in war, and begging only for the mercy of her brothers, and promising submission forever.*

This thing—as the human heart is inclined to *spare the subjected and battle the proud* <note>original: "parcere subiectis & debellare superbos" — a famous maxim from Virgil’s *Aeneid* describing the Roman approach to mercy and power</note>, and to be moved to pity by the miseries of others—*will also bend the Boar toward mercy, so that he may establish peace between her and her brothers, according to the laws of nature.* Therefore, when for the sake of exploring the truth he approaches her too incautiously with his own men, *she, by no means forgetting her innate fraud—with ambushes perhaps arranged, as is common in such opportune places, in traps—will bite his left foot*, [catchword: tot]

This man, by managing and supporting the Boar's affairs in many worldly matters, will seem to carry him, in a way, like a foot, since he renders the Boar secure and free from such cares.

But the Fox will snatch away this friend, who was so necessary and faithful to him, by capturing him and, as it were, tearing him from the Boar's body. Not content with this, *having made a leap, she will snatch away his right ear and his tail*; that is to say, his "right-hand" counselor—one who gives good and useful advice—and his "tail," which represents his following army <note>The "tail" of a leader traditionally refers to the retinue or soldiers that follow behind.</note>. When all these things have been perpetrated through fraud rather than through strength, *she will hide herself within the caverns of the mountains*; that is, she will retreat into her castles and fortifications.

*The Boar, therefore, having been mocked, will seek out the Bear and the Wolf so that they might restore his lost limbs to him*—meaning, his captives. # THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

*...will change into a wolf. And as if she were about to hold a conversation with the boar, she will approach him and craftily devour him whole.* This scene of deceit could be carried out in the following way: the fox might send some of the wolf's own household and close friends—corrupted by money or some other means—to the boar. They would act in the wolf’s name, inviting the boar to meet the wolf for a talk. The boar, unaware of the ambush, will encounter the fox instead of the wolf and be immediately killed by her along with all his followers, so that no one remains to report the deed. This is indeed what the prophecy means when it says, *she will craftily devour the whole boar.* 

Once this betrayal is finished, and before the fraud committed against the boar is discovered, she could use those same household members—now traitors—to call her own brothers, the wolves, as if to talk with the boar, similarly using the boar’s name and identity. The wolves, not at all distrustful of their own household and friends, will encounter the fox instead of the boar and be caught in the same disaster, killed by the fox. This is what the prophecy says: *Then—that is, after the boar has been killed—she will transform herself into the boar and, as if she were without limbs, she will wait for her brothers. But even them, after they have arrived, she will suddenly kill with her tooth and she will be crowned with the head of the Lion.* 

This means that she will take on the ferocity of the Lion—who is the king of beasts and fears no encounter—and, confident that no one can resist her, she will place the crown of the kingdom upon her head like a Lion. *In his days, a serpent will be born who will threaten the death of mortals. He shall join to himself the flocks of Scotland and Wales, who shall dry up the Thames by drinking.* As much as can be understood from these words—partly figurative, partly clear enough—he suggests the King of **Scotland** <note>original: "Albania", the Gaelic name for Scotland</note>, who, having taken up the head of a wolf (that is, having allied himself with the King of **Wales** <note>original: "Cambria"</note>), is set to lead an army against **London**.

Indeed, he calls the King of **Scotland** a "mountain bull," as the following words declare: a "bull" because of his weightiness or slowness, and "mountainous" because, as I have already said above, that entire region is full of mountains. Moreover, he calls the King of **Wales** the "head of a wolf." For **Wales**, as I mentioned before, is full of groves and forests in which is the dwelling-place of wolves. This is a figurative way of speaking which the Greeks call <term>metonymy: a figure of speech where a thing or concept is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it</term>, by which the thing contained is put for the container, or the container for the thing contained.

*Therefore the mountain bull shall take up the head of a wolf,* that is, he shall associate the prince of **Wales** with himself, *and shall whiten his teeth in the forge of the Severn,* that is, he shall sharpen and file them. He calls the fortifications of **Wales** the "forge of the **Severn**." For the **Severn** <note>original: "Sabrina"</note> is a river on the borders of **Wales**, from which the **Severn Sea** <note>the Bristol Channel</note> takes its name. There, therefore, the mountain bull shall whiten his teeth—namely, by sharpening the dullness of his own laziness and spirit with the sharpness of the **Welsh**, and by scraping away the rust of his own slowness with their eagerness. *The mountain bull shall take up the head of a wolf, and his teeth in*

<margin>2 Chronicles chapter 18</margin>

<margin>The Swan.</margin>
The **swan** is a river bird, and is considered a lucky omen among sailors. For they expect a prosperous course through the dangers of the sea when they see one, for the reason that it never dives under the water. Thus says the poet **Aemilius**: <note>original: "Æmilius Poëta" — Likely Aemilius Macer, a Roman poet whose works on birds and nature were frequently cited in the Middle Ages.</note>

> The swan is always the most joyful bird in omens,
> Sailors desire it, for it does not sink into the waves;

This bird sometimes dwells in the waters and sometimes lives on the land. For throughout the summer and in all warm seasons, it floats upon the rivers. In winter, however, when the waters freeze over, it comes out and lives on the seeds of crops on the land. Therefore, when he says: *The ashes of that king shall be changed into swans, who shall swim on dry land as if in a river*, it signifies that his descendants—now indeed living on the sea—will rob or kill everyone they meet through **pirate attacks**, <note>original: "pyratica infestatione" — A reference to maritime raiding, common in the history of the British Isles and Brittany.</note> as the following words show, and at other times they will plague the fatherland with battles on land. 

Hence it follows: *They will devour fish among fish, and swallow men among men.* For because it is against the nature of swans to devour fish—since they are not fed on fish, but on herbs or grains—therefore when he had said, *They will devour fish among fish*, he added, *and they will swallow men among men.* By these words, he clearly shows that he was not speaking of literal swan-birds, but of men under the figure of swans, who will range about with such great savagery—

He was the one who—after the young King of the Britons, *Constans*, was killed at *London* by his own household and mercenary soldiers from the *Picts*—seized the crown of the kingdom by force, as there was no one who could resist him (meaning *Vortigern*). And when he was pressed by the most heavy invasions from his neighbors, namely the *Picts* and the *Scots*, he invited the *Saxons* into the island to his aid. Therefore, these *Gewisseans*, who serve the *Londoners* and the *Mercians* <note>original: "Mertiis"</note>, will rouse the *North Welsh*, that is the *Welsh*, to take up arms against them. And this is what he means when he says: *The oaks of the forests shall come together, and shall clash with the stones of the Gewisseans*; that is, with the strongest peoples of the *Gewisseans*, who are most hard like stones in their endurance of all labors.

# THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

*The raven shall fly with the kites, and shall devour the bodies of the slain.* <note>original: "Advolabit corvus cum Miluis, & corpora peremptorum devorabit."</note> As if to say: So great shall be the slaughter of men that ravens and kites <note>A "kite" is a type of hawk known for scavenging.</note> will gather from every side to devour the corpses of those killed. There follows: *An owl shall nest upon the walls of Gloucester, and in its nest an ass shall be brought forth. The serpent of Malvern shall raise him, and shall stir him to many deceits. Having taken the crown, he shall transcend the heights, and shall terrify the people of the country with his horrible braying.* <note>original: "Super muros Claudioceftriæ nidificabit bubo... horrido recanatu populum patriae terrebit."</note> Gloucester <note>original: "Claudioceftria"</note> took its name from Claudius Caesar; it was enlarged by Arvirargus, King of the Britons and son-in-law to Claudius himself, in the place where he took Genuissa, the daughter of Claudius, as his wife; and in memory and honor of Claudius, he named it Gloucester.

<margin>The Owl.</margin> The owl is a bird associated with death and is considered filthy, and in the taking of omens, it is always unlucky. For wherever it appears, it signifies that devastation and mourning are at hand for that place. <margin>Ovid.</margin> Whence Ovid says: *A foul bird, the herald of coming grief. The unhappy owl, a dire omen for mortals.* <note>original: "foedáq; volucris, venturi nuntia luctus. Infelix bubo dirum mortalibus omen."</note> Its name is given to it from the sound of its voice, according to the figure of speech which they call <term>Onomatopoeia</term> <note>A term for words that imitate the natural sounds of a thing.</note>. Just as the name "crane" <note>original: "grus"</note> comes from its cry, or the "clangor" of trumpets, and "tinkling." Whence it is said in the poet: *To burn the stubble with crackling flames.* <note>original: "Stipulam crepitantibus urere flammis." — a reference to Virgil's Georgics.</note> And that of the Apostle, <margin>1 Corinthians 13:1</margin> *I shall be like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal.* So also there: *And the hinges of the temple shall creak.* <margin>Amos 8:3</margin> To this figure of speech some wish to assign the roaring of lions, the bleating of sheep, the lowing of cattle, and similar sounds. The owl is also a <term>nocturnal bird</term> <note>original: "ales nocturnus"</note>, because, like the night-owls, it keeps watch at night and sleeps during the day, and it possesses large eyes.

[The owl] loves the mists of darkness and shrinks from the sun's splendor; and in a wondrous manner—contrary to the nature of almost all other birds and animals—it is blinded by the brightness of day but illuminated by the shadows of night. Such are the crafty men of this age: cunning in evil, but foolish and dull in what is good; and, to use the words of the prophet, *they are wise to do evil, but they know not how to do good* <note>original: "sapientes ut faciant mala, bene autem facere nescientes"</note>.
<margin>Jeremiah 4, verse 22.</margin>
They are sharp and subtle for acting wickedly, but blunt and dull for acting well. Therefore, according to these abominable and perverse properties of the owl that we have listed—and any others there may be—consider that prince whom Merlin thought should be marked by the name "owl," for no other reason than the great affinity and likeness he will have with that bird. Imagine him, therefore, to be a ravager of the fatherland and the author and messenger of total desolation and mourning; crafty and shrewd in perpetrating crimes, but senseless and foolish in doing good works. Therefore, following the metaphor of the owl, which is accustomed to living in the holes and caverns of towers and walls and hides during the day, *Merlin says that an owl shall nest upon the walls of Gloucester, and in its nest an ass shall be brought forth* <note>original: "super muros Claudioceftriæ nidificabit bubo, & in nido suo procreabitur asinus"</note>; *that is, a foolish and undisciplined son, utterly unworthy of royal honor.* And lest you think our interpretation of this chapter is forced or far-fetched, you should know that even today, in common human speech, it is frequently said of children—and especially of the dull and lazy—"*this is that man's egg, and he...*"

For sandy and solid places are not subject to these tremors, whereas cavernous places are. 

This is also why Sicily—because it is almost entirely hollow and layered with sulfur and bitumen—is open almost everywhere to winds and fires, with the internal spirit <note>A reference to the classical theory that earthquakes and volcanoes were caused by trapped wind or "spiritus" struggling to escape the earth.</note> struggling within. This is why, in many places, it often belches smoke and vapors or even flames; or, when the wind presses more sharply, it casts out masses of sand and stones, just as Virgil shows in the third book

But someone might say that "worm" is used for "worms"—the singular number for the plural, in fact. This figure of speech the Greeks call <term>syllepsis: a rhetorical figure where a singular noun is used to represent a collective group, or vice-versa</term>, which is indeed a very frequent figure both among the secular orators and in the divine books as well: namely, when either one is put for many, or many for one. One, for example, is put for many,
<margin>Psalm 77 verse 47</margin> as in the Psalm where it is said: *He sent among them the dog-fly and it consumed them, and the frog and it destroyed them.* 
<note>original: "Miſit in eos Cynomiã & comedit eos, & ranam & disperdidit eos." The author is pointing out that the Latin uses the singular "rana" (frog) to describe a plague of many frogs.</note>
Conversely, 
<margin>Psalm 2</margin> many are put for one, as in that place: *The kings of the earth stood up and the princes gathered together into one, against the Lord and against his Christ.* 
<note>original: "Aſtiterunt Reges terræ & principes conuenerunt in unum..."</note>
For the Apostles understood "Kings" to be put for Herod, and "Princes" for Pilate,
<margin>Acts ch. 4 verse 24</margin> as is shown in the Acts of the Apostles, where the believers, with one mind with the Apostles, lifted their voice to the Lord and said: *Lord, you who said through the mouth of David your servant: Why did the nations rage and the people meditate on vain things? The kings of the earth stood up and...*

# THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

...[meta]phor <note>original: "phoram," likely the end of "metaphoram"</note> of goats, he speaks of this in his usual manner; the power of their breath is so great that when it is inhaled by she-goats, the females are inflamed for mating. Nor is this surprising, since Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a Roman geographer from the 3rd or 4th century whose work was a popular source for medieval "natural history."</note> affirms that certain mares in Cappadocia conceive from the mere scent of male horses, and especially from the stallions. He says the same of partridges: that lust so agitates them that if the wind blows from a male, they are impregnated by the scent alone. *Therefore, those seven lions shall go forth from the aforementioned worm, disfigured with the heads of goats, which shall corrupt women with the stench of their nostrils.* As for what he says about that worm—that *it shall despoil the provinces of their forests and burn the trees by emitting a fiery vapor*—it seems to me to have this meaning: namely, that to open a path for himself through countless wooded places and to clear the way, he himself will, as often happens, cut down and burn the forests. For he shall climb upon the dragon and, having cast off his garment, he shall sit upon him naked. The dragon shall carry him to the heights, and with its tail raised, it shall lash the naked man. But with his strength recovered, the giant shall smash the dragon's jaws with a sword. The dragon shall be entangled under its own tail and shall perish poisoned.* Giants, just as they excel other men in the vastness of their bodies and the great keenness of their sight, are able to look upon and survey distant regions of the earth—far removed from the common sight of men—with total ease. <meta>This page continues the interpretation of the prophecy of Merlin. The previous page discussed the "worm" that destroys forests and the seven lions with goat heads who corrupt the land. ### BOOK VI. 239

Following his custom, he does not name him directly, but designates him antonomastically <note>original: "antonomasticè"; a rhetorical device where a person is described by their attributes or a title rather than their proper name</note> by his characteristics. He says that a tall and immense figure of giant-like height will arrive—a master of wickedness and malice—who will terrify everyone with the sharpness of his eyes, for they will find no way to escape his gaze or hide from him.

<margin>Varro. See Pliny, Book 7, Chapter 21. Strabo, Book 6. Satellicus, Book 9. Ennius, Book 4. Valerius Maximus, Book 1, Chapter 8. Regarding Strabo, see also Lynceus and Aelian, Book 11, *On Various History*.</margin>
Thus Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, an ancient Roman scholar</note> recounts that a certain man named Strabo had such powerful eyesight that he could see beyond one hundred and thirty-five miles. It was his habit, when the Punic fleet <note>The navy of Carthage, Rome's great rival</note> departed from Carthage against the Romans, to most clearly count the number of ships from the Lilybean lookout <note>original: "Lilybetana specula"; a watchtower or high point at Cape Lilybaeum in Sicily, the point closest to North Africa</note>. For this reason, his watchfulness was a cause of great fear to the Carthaginians, because on account of him, they were unable to surprise the Romans or find them unprepared through any sudden or secret approach. "*He shall come upon them,*" he says, "*the giant of wickedness, who shall terrify everyone with the sharpness of his eyes.*"

Who are these "everyone"? Specifically, the seven lions disfigured with the heads of goats, who shall be born from the worm that burns the trees of the province, and who shall corrupt women with the stench of their nostrils, making those who should be wives to individuals into common property. This was once a custom among many barbarian peoples, and especially among the Garamantes <note>An ancient tribal civilization in the Libyan Sahara</note> dwelling in Africa, where they were joined by no legitimate marriage but copulated in a beastly manner, so that only the mothers could recognize their own children. To this beastly and communal lust, therefore, the aforementioned lions with goat heads will reduce the people of the country. "*Over these, therefore, shall come the giant of wickedness, and everyone...*"

# THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

...with his aids *he will terrify with the sharpness of his eyes. There shall arise against him the dragon of Worcester, and he will endeavor to exterminate him.* Worcester <note>original: "Vigornia"</note> is a certain city of Britain, situated upon the Severn <note>original: "Sabrinam"</note>. From there, therefore, the dragon will go forth who will endeavor to exterminate the giant of wickedness—that is, to expel him from the borders. The word "dragon" <note>original: "Draco"</note> is derived from the Greek word *derkein* <note>δέρκειν; to see clearly</note>, that is, from the act of seeing, because it sees more sharply than other living 
<margin>Dragon.</margin> creatures. Similarly, there is the wild animal which is called a *dorcas* <note>a gazelle or antelope, likewise named for its bright eyes</note>. The dragon is a serpent larger than all living creatures; it is without feet, rests in caves, and is lifted up into the air. For there are certain dragons that are winged and fly through the air. 
<margin>Isidore.</margin> Whence Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar whose "Etymologies" served as a standard encyclopedia for the Middle Ages</note> says: *The dragon, he says, is the largest of all serpents, and indeed of all animals upon the earth. Frequently drawn out from its caves, it is borne into the air, and the air is agitated because of it. It is crested, with a small mouth and narrow pipes through which it draws its breath and thrusts out its tongue. Its strength, however, is not in its teeth, but in its tail. It is harmless in terms of venom, but for that reason, venoms are not necessary for it to inflict death; for if it binds anyone, it kills them, and even the elephant is not made safe from it by the vast size of its body. For lurking around the paths through which elephants are accustomed to walk, it entangles and binds their legs with its coils, and so destroys them by suffocation.* The dragon does harm by the lash of its tail rather than by a bite. The sea-dragon has a sting in its fins <note>original: "brachiis"; literally "arms"</note> pointing toward the tail. *The dragon of Worcester shall rise against him, and shall endeavor to exterminate him.* He is called a "dragon" because of certain similarities which he will share with the dragon.

### BOOK VI

A dragon of such a kind, under the same figure of speech, was that Pharaoh, the King of Egypt, as we read in the Prophet: *the great dragon, who lay in the midst of the rivers and said, the rivers are mine, and I made them.* <margin>Ezekiel ch. 29 v. 3</margin> The **Dragon of Worcester** <note>original: "Draco Vigorniæ"</note> will rise up against him and will endeavor to exterminate him. However, once the battle is joined, the dragon will be overcome, and he will be crushed by the wickedness of the man and the giant. For he will mount the dragon—that is, he will subject the dragon to himself—and, having stripped off his clothes, he will sit upon him naked. This is spoken according to the metaphor of a dragon. For there are dragons of this sort that are winged and fly through the air, breathing fire <note>original: "flammiuomi," literally "flame-vomiting"</note>, who burn whatever they approach with their fiery breath. The dragon will carry him to high places, having seemed to prevail for a time, and will crush the giant according to his whim, and will seem to have almost conquered him. The dragon will carry him to high places, and with an erect tail will strike the naked man. This is said according to the specific nature of the dragon, which, as we said above, strikes more with its tail than it wounds with a bite. 

But when the dragon has seemed to himself to have nearly gained hold of the giant and to have overcome him, having achieved victory, suddenly the giant, with his strengths resumed and his audacity recalled, will kill the dragon with a sword. And this is what follows: *Resuming his vigor again, the **Giant** will shatter his jaws*—namely the dragon’s—*with a sword. At last, the dragon will be entangled under his own tail, and will perish poisoned.* For the venom, as was said above, is held in the tail, not in the teeth. Moreover, regarding what he says—*at last, the dragon will be entangled under his own tail, and will perish poisoned*—we can understand this either as spoken according to the metaphor of a dragon, like the other parts, or certainly we may take his "tail" to mean a following army, among whom,

For a certain man, more reckless than the others and more impudent than all, climbed the walls and bared his loins <note>original: "inguina sua nudauit"</note>; in contempt of the Duke and the entire army, he began to make foul cracks <note>original: "immundos crepitus"; referring to flatulence as an insult</note> from his posterior. For these men are irreverent, and therefore destitute of God's help." Having said these things, as they began to arm themselves, the wall of the city immediately collapsed (a wonder to behold), and opened the town to the victorious people without the need for spear or bow.

### THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

...we have gathered, the sum of which is this: that under the various names and types of serpents, and the mention of the battles and slaughters they wage among themselves, the prophecies signify the most dreadful wars and deaths of men against one another. Nevertheless, let us treat each individual chapter, at least with a brief and succinct interpretation, according to our custom. *She shall surround it, he says:* there is no doubt that this refers to the fox of Carlisle <note>original: "Caerdubali"</note>, which, in revenge for the lion, shall break its horns against the walls of Exeter <note>original: "Exoniæ"</note> upon the bull, and shall consume it entirely with its teeth. *The serpent of Lincoln <note>original: "Lindicolinus coluber"</note> shall therefore come upon this fox*, that is, it shall bite or strike it; meaning the serpent proceeding from the city of Lincoln. 

A serpent <note>original: "Coluber"</note> is so called, according to the etymology of the name, because it "inhabits shadows" <note>original: "umbras colat"; a medieval folk etymology linking "coluber" (serpent) with "colere" (to inhabit) and "umbra" (shadow)</note>, or because it glides into slippery paths with winding coils. For that is called "slippery" <note>original: "lubricum"</note> which slips away while being held, like an eel, a small lamprey, or a snake. Thus, this "Lincolnite" will be slippery—whoever he may be—who comes upon the fox; that is, who bites and strikes it. 

Such a serpent was Ahaz, King of Judah. At whose death, when his enemies the Philistines rejoiced, the word of the Lord came by the hand of Isaiah, saying to them: *"Rejoice not, all you of Philistia, because the rod of him that struck you is broken. For out of the root of the serpent shall come forth a basilisk <note>original: "regulus"; literally "little king," often used for a basilisk or venomous serpent</note>, and his seed shall swallow the flying one"* <note>A translation of Isaiah 14:29</note>. Here he calls Ahaz the serpent, and Hezekiah his son the basilisk. And because the *coluber* is a species of snake, this must be known generally: they are called "serpents" <note>original: "serpentes"</note> because they "crawl" <note>original: "serpentes", from the verb "serpere"</note> by hidden approaches...

While it is true that all serpents are reptiles, because they crawl <note>original: "reptant"</note> on their belly and chest, not all reptiles are serpents. This is spoken according to a certain characteristic of the serpent. For the serpent, as they say, while it boldly attacks a clothed man, it fears a naked one and does not dare to approach him to do harm. <note>This reflects a common medieval bestiary belief that snakes were intimidated by human skin but emboldened by clothing.</note> Furthermore, just as there is no doubt that under the metaphor of serpents and dragons, the discourse concerns men who are like serpents and dragons, according to that saying of the blessed

> Job: *I was a brother to dragons, and a companion to ostriches*, <note>original: "frater fui draconum, & socius strutionum"</note>

we hold it as certain and evident to the eyes that many who have been despoiled of their own property by enemies and stripped bare, or even had their goods given to the fire, work more fiercely by whatever art, by whatever machinations, and in whatever manner to avenge themselves upon their adversaries. Thus, they frequently overwhelm or kill those against whom they previously had no power while they were "clothed"—that is, while they were invested with their possessions and external goods and had suffered no loss at the hands of men. Hence it was said above, concerning the giant of wickedness <note>original: "gigante nequitiæ"</note> who shall fight with the dragon of Worcester, <note>original: "Vigorniæ"; the Latin name for Worcester.</note> that he shall only then prevail against the dragon and shatter its jaws with a sword when, his clothing having been burned (doubtless by the fire of the dragon), he should mount the dragon naked and sit upon its back. This, therefore, is what is said here:

> *His clothing burned, he shall mount another, and cast his right hand and his left upon the tail.*

It follows: *A giant shall shine with snowy whiteness, and shall bring forth a white people.* He who was first a lion is now a giant—but not that "giant of wickedness" <note>original: "gigas nequitiæ"</note> of whom he spoke above, saying, *The giant of wickedness shall come, who shall terrify everyone with the sharpness of his eyes.* For this giant, honored by snowy whiteness—that is, by venerable gray hair <note>original: "veneranda canitie"; the Latin "canities" refers specifically to the gray or white hair of old age, symbolizing wisdom.</note>—shall not terrify the people, but shall govern them with kind gentleness and treat them with all peace and tranquility. And this is what he means when he says he shall bring forth a "white" people: namely, that his lion-like ferocity has been set aside and a snowy whiteness assumed. For we can understand this snowy whiteness in which he shall shine as being not only the outer whiteness of the body, but also the inner maturity of the mind—that venerable grayness of which it is said:

# BOOK VI.

...of infants with blood. Then there shall be a **fish in the sea**, which, called back by the hiss of a serpent, shall mate with it. As I understand it, this will be a **Lamprey** <note>original: "Muræna"</note>; however, this is by way of symbolic meaning, not by its literal nature.

<margin>The Lamprey.</margin>
The Lamprey is a fish which in Latin is called *Lampreda*. It is called *Murena* in Greek, however, because it folds itself into many circles. This creature has its life <note>original: "animam," literally "soul" or "life-force"</note> not in its head, but in its tail. This is proven by the fact that if its head is crushed, it can hardly be killed; but if its tail is struck, it is immediately weakened and dies. It is said, moreover, that the Lamprey is a relative of the serpent, because it mates with the serpent. How this comes to pass is well worth the effort to see. 

When a serpent is inflamed for mating, it calls out to the Lamprey—whether it be a male calling a female, or a female calling a male. Having heard the serpent's hiss, the Lamprey rises to the surface of the water. However, upon seeing the serpent, it is naturally terrified of its venom; not daring to approach or mingle with it, the Lamprey returns beneath the waters and hides itself from the serpent’s sight. 

But the serpent, driven by the sting of lust, hisses again and calls the Lamprey back into its presence. The Lamprey, seeing it again, is afraid and flees. This continues for a long time, until the serpent, unable to endure the heat of its desire any further, offers the Lamprey "hostages of peace and innocence" <note>This is a vivid medieval metaphor for the serpent temporarily setting aside its lethal nature to attract a mate.</note> by vomiting out its venom. It will, however, take back and swallow this venom again after mating, because a serpent cannot live without its poison. And so, the Lamprey, having been made more secure, approaches and mingles with the serpent. For this reason, many people [avoid] the eating of the Lamprey—that is, the *Lampreda*—as if it were the eating of a serpent...

# THE PROPHECIES OF MERLIN

...of the city, of whom the fables of the poets relate that by the sound of the lyre <note>original: "cytharæ"</note> and the sweetness of music, he moved stones from their place, attracted them to himself, and made them come together for the work of a building. This, according to the literal sense, is in no way likely to have happened in such a manner; rather, he was a wise man, and since he was eloquent in his words and spoke with refined and pleasant sweetness, he enticed wild men and dwellers among the rocks, who were rude in their uncultivated habits, to build a city and at the same time to live under the law, according to the discipline of rational laws. 
<margin>Horace.</margin>
Whence Horace says:

> *Orpheus, the sacred interpreter of the gods,*
> *Deterred wild men from slaughter and a foul diet.*
> *On this account, he was said to soothe tigers and raging lions.*
> *Amphion too, the founder of the Theban city, was said*
> *To move stones by the sound of his lyre and by enticing prayer,*
> *To lead them where he wished. This was wisdom in former times:*
> *To separate public from private, and sacred from profane things;*
> *To prohibit wandering intercourse, and to grant laws to husbands.*

...however, in various and diverse ways, according to the nature of the times. Indeed, those things which have unfolded down to our own times, I have brought out of the darkness into the light—by a faithful explanation, as far as I judge—in accordance with the truth of histories and the outcome of events. Furthermore, regarding those things which are to come after us—since histories do not prophesy the future but rather narrate what has already been done, and it is one thing to be a historian and another to be a seer <note>original: "vates"; a divinely inspired poet or prophet</note>—I have not followed the chronological sequence of histories. 

Instead, I have devoted myself to investigating the meaning of his sayings according to the tropes of prophetic speech, the meanings and figures of words, and also according to the natures and properties of the things themselves from which he draws his metaphors. He often calls people by the names of these things rather than by their proper names. Moreover, I have followed the idiom and manner of speaking which I have perceived him to maintain through the whole context of his work by skillful investigation. I have invented nothing from my own heart that is discordant, absurd, forced, or foreign to the customary and usual translation of words <note>The author is defending his method, claiming he isn't making things up but following established linguistic patterns</note>. Any studious and diligent reader will be able to notice this well enough, provided they approach the reading and subsequent judgment with a benevolent mind, and do not think they must travel a path wasted by envy.

Now indeed, in this final and most recent little book which I now begin, it falls to me to explain, as best I can, the latest and final prophecies of the same Merlin—specifically concerning the signs which, as the end of the world <note>original: "mundi termino"</note> approaches...

<margin>1. Saturn</margin>

The sixth is **Mercury**, completing its course in the traversal of the Zodiac with an orbit swifter by nine days <note>The text specifies "9 days" (*9. diebus*), which may refer to a specific astronomical calculation or a scribal error regarding Mercury's rapid 88-day orbital period relative to other planets.</note>, and shining now before the rising of the sun, and now after its setting.

The seventh is the **Moon**, much closer to the Earth than the other planets. For this reason, it completes its course more quickly in a shorter circle. For the journey which the **Sun** completes in 365 days, the **Moon** runs through in 30 days. Therefore, the ancients placed the months in the course of the **Moon**, but the years in the course of the **Sun**.

Furthermore, each of the planets has its own individual circles, which the Greeks call **apsides** <term>absides|the points in an orbit closest or farthest from the center of motion</term>, according to the certain logic of the compass, so that they rise from their own center to their own apogee. For this reason, they also have diverse circles and dissimilar movements, since it is necessary for the inner orbits to be shorter. Therefore, from the center of the Earth, the highest points of the orbits <note>original: *absides altissimæ*</note> are: for **Saturn** in **Scorpio**, for **Jupiter** in **Virgo**, for **Mars** in **Leo**, for the **Sun** in **Gemini**, for **Venus** in **Sagittarius**, for **Mercury** in **Capricorn**, and for the **Moon** in **Taurus**.

These figures were elevated to the heavens by the poets in their songs because some of them were inventors and masters of the arts, such as **Aesculapius** in the field of medicine.

There were also brave men and founders of cities; after they died, the people who had loved them fashioned statues <note>original: *simulachra*</note>, so that they might have some comfort from contemplating their images. However, through the persuasion of demons, this honor gradually turned into superstition, to such an extent that those whom the ancients had honored solely to preserve the memory of their names were regarded as gods by their successors.

Furthermore, the poets—through the elegance of their words and the sweetness of their speech—convinced foolish men that these mortals had been made immortal. Indeed, they went even further, claiming that some humans were turned into stars, others into trees, animals, flowers, and birds, or into springs and rivers. They asserted that almost all stars, trees, flowers, and rivers were once human.

By way of example, let us demonstrate at least one of each of these transformations. They say that **Andromeda**, daughter of Cepheus <note>The Latin text says *Cerei*, which is likely a scribal variant or error for *Cephei* (of Cepheus).</note>, was turned into a star. Likewise, the brothers **Castor** and **Pollux** were changed into the constellations called the **Gemini**. So too was **Callisto** turned into a star, which <term>catasterism|the process of a person or object being transformed into a star or constellation</term>...
